name: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar
summary: The hatted, ocean-front Italian fine-diner perched above the Bondi Icebergs pool, serving hand-rolled pasta and seasonal seafood with the best beach view in Sydney.
whyGo: This is Bondi's special-occasion benchmark, and we'd send anyone here for the combination you genuinely can't get anywhere else: a menu of modern Italian cooking that has held a chef's hat almost continuously since 2002, framed by a wall of glass over the famous ocean pool and the Pacific beyond. Maurice Terzini's room is polished without being stuffy, and the kitchen leans on hand-made pasta, sustainably sourced seafood and carefully chosen produce rather than gimmicks. It rewards a booking and a bit of an occasion.
bestFor: Milestone celebrations and long lunches with a view
whatToOrder: Hand-rolled seasonal pasta and the sustainably sourced seafood are the signatures; the fixed-price choice set menu is the reliable way in, and vegetarian, vegan and children's menus are offered alongside the a la carte.
atmosphere: Elegant, buzzy and light-filled, with an unbeatable outlook over the Icebergs pool and Bondi's south end.
localTip: Book a window table for lunch rather than dinner - you'll pay similar money but get the full sweep of the pool, the beach and the surf in daylight, which is the whole point of coming here. If you can't get a table, the separate bar takes walk-ins for a cocktail and the same view.
tradeOff: It's genuinely expensive (set menus run well over $100pp) and firmly a dress-up, book-ahead occasion rather than a casual post-beach drop-in.

name: Sean's
summary: A Bondi institution since 1993 where chef-owner Sean Moran serves a daily-changing, produce-driven three-course choice menu above a panoramic sweep of Campbell Parade and the beach.
whyGo: This is the grande dame of Bondi dining, and one of the few tables here built entirely around seasonality rather than a beachside crowd. The short chalkboard menu changes as often as daily, much of it grown at Moran's own farm in the Blue Mountains, and the cooking is deceptively simple home-style food executed with real precision. We'd choose it when you want the beach setting to come with genuine substance on the plate rather than just a view.
bestFor: A special-occasion long lunch or unhurried dinner with a view
whatToOrder: It's a set three-course choice menu (three options per course) that turns over with the season, so go by what's on the board that day rather than a fixed dish; expect vegetable-forward, produce-led plates and honest home-style cooking.
atmosphere: Warm, convivial and refined-but-relaxed, with an upstairs dining room and terrace open to the panorama.
localTip: Our pick is a weekend lunch (served Friday to Sunday) so you get the full daylight panorama across the beach; book ahead, as the room is intimate and this is a long-running favourite.
tradeOff: It's a premium fixed three-course menu, not a casual walk-in for a quick bite, and lunch runs only Friday to Sunday.

name: Gelato Messina Bondi
address: G6/61 Hall Street, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: The Bondi outpost of Sydney's most celebrated gelato maker, tucked into the Hall Street hub a short walk back from the sand.
whyGo: Messina is the benchmark for gelato in Sydney, and the Bondi store pours the same 40-odd house-churned flavours and rotating weekly specials as the flagship, made with genuine care (house-roasted hazelnuts, Warrnambool milk). We'd choose this over any beachfront soft-serve when you want the real thing after a swim. The room itself is worth a look too, designed to feel like an upside-down swimming pool with pebblecrete walls and ceiling.
bestFor: A post-beach dessert walk on Hall Street
whatToOrder: A scoop or two from the signature range, one of the always-changing weekly specials, or a whole handmade gelato cake if you're feeding a crowd; sorbets cover the dairy-free crowd.
atmosphere: Buzzy, queue-out-the-door on warm evenings, order-at-the-counter
localTip: It's on Hall Street rather than right on the promenade, so grab your cone here and stroll it down to the beach or Bondi Park rather than expecting a sea view from the door. Go for a weekly special before it rotates out.
tradeOff: It's a takeaway counter with little seating and no beach outlook, and queues get long at peak times on hot days.

name: Hotel Ravesis
summary: An iconic 1914 beachfront hotel on Campbell Parade whose light-filled level-one dining room now houses Alzado, a coastal-Spanish seafood diner, above a classic public bar and late-night club space.
whyGo: This is the only hotel sitting directly on the Bondi beachfront with uninterrupted ocean views, and its arched 1914 windows frame the sand better than almost anywhere else on the strip. The dining room reopened in late 2025 as Alzado, a coastal-Spanish restaurant built around just-caught seafood, the plancha and a serious vermouth-and-sherry list, so you get a genuine destination meal rather than a tired hotel menu. Downstairs a beachside public bar and an upstairs club room mean the building carries you from an afternoon aperitivo through to a late night.
bestFor: A long, view-soaked afternoon that turns into a night out
whatToOrder: Lean into the plancha and share plates: whole grilled squid or sardines, house-preserved albacore, croquetas, pan con tomate with anchovies, and a sirloin to share with fries — start with an oyster-shell gin martini.
atmosphere: Sun-washed, holiday coastal-Spain by day; lively and clubby after dark.
localTip: Book a window or terrace table at Alzado for the golden hour before sunset — that top-floor light off the water is the whole point of being here, and it goes fast in summer.
tradeOff: It's an elevated, share-style spend with a bar-and-club energy rather than a quiet or especially kid-focused dinner.

name: bills Bondi Beach
summary: The original bills, the Hall Street cafe where Bill Granger reinvented Sydney brunch, still turning out its ricotta hotcakes and creamy scrambled eggs a couple of minutes back from the sand.
whyGo: This is where the modern Sydney brunch was effectively invented, and the dishes that made bills famous have never left the menu. We'd choose it when you want a genuine piece of Bondi food history rather than just a beachfront table, and it holds up all day, moving from communal-table breakfasts into a proper lunch and evening service. It is a destination cafe, so expect it to be busy and priced accordingly.
bestFor: A landmark Bondi brunch a short walk from the beach
whatToOrder: The signatures are the reason to come: the ricotta hotcakes with honeycomb butter and banana, the sweetcorn fritters, and the famously creamy scrambled eggs.
atmosphere: Bright, buzzy and communal, built around bills' trademark big shared table.
localTip: It's on Hall Street rather than the promenade, so if you're coming straight off the beach it's a two-minute walk up from the sand; bookings only kick in from 5pm, so for the famous breakfast plan to arrive early or be ready to wait for a walk-in table on weekends.
tradeOff: No ocean views and premium cafe pricing, and weekend queues for a table are the norm.

name: Alzado
address: Level 1, 118 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A Spanish coastal seafood diner upstairs at Hotel Ravesis, trading share plates, sherry and oyster martinis against a wraparound balcony view of the Bondi surf.
whyGo: Alzado takes the first floor of the landmark Ravesis corner and turns it into an all-afternoon Iberian holiday, with a menu built around Barcelona, Madrid and San Sebastian by exec chef Pablo Tordesillas (ex-Ortiga) and head chef MJ Olguera. It is elevated but deliberately not formal, engineered for the long lunch that rolls into a golden-hour dinner. We'd choose this when you want the beachfront-with-a-view occasion without the stiffness of fine dining.
bestFor: Long boozy lunches and sunset dinners with a view
whatToOrder: Start with jamon croquetas and pan con tomate (worth the Cantabrian anchovy or jamon Iberico add-on), then plancha-grilled squid or sardines; for the table, the brothy seafood rice (arroz caldoso) or lamb belly ribs, and the 1kg Kidman rib eye if you're a group. Drinks are the point too: oyster martinis, sherry and vermouth on ice.
atmosphere: Sun-soaked, lively and casually sophisticated on a wraparound beachfront balcony.
localTip: Book the balcony for late afternoon rather than peak dinner: the aperitivo window catches the golden sunset over the sand, and the share-plate menu is made for grazing before the evening rush fills the room.
tradeOff: It's a $$$ share-plate format, so a full spread with the pricier seafood and steak adds up fast, and the buzzy first-floor room leans lively rather than quiet or intimate.

name: Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta
address: The Hub, Shop LG08 & LG09, 75-79 Hall Street, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A buzzy Hall Street institution serving wood-fired Neapolitan pizza and rotisserie porchetta, back in its original Bondi home under founder Orazio D'Elia.
whyGo: This is one of Bondi's most enduring Italian rooms — opened in 2014, bought back and relaunched by Orazio D'Elia in 2022, and awarded a Good Food Guide Chef's Hat. The draw is genuinely good Neapolitan-style wood-fired pizza alongside the signature focaccia with rotisserie porchetta, in a lively 90-seat room a short walk up from the sand. With the sister bar Orazietto next door, we'd send anyone here who wants a proper sit-down Italian dinner rather than a quick beach feed.
bestFor: A lively Italian dinner with friends or a couple, a short walk from the beach.
whatToOrder: The wood-fired Neapolitan pizzas (the Margherita is the honest test of any kitchen) and the signature focaccia con porchetta; antipasti share plates and seafood pasta round out a table.
atmosphere: Warm, packed and buzzy — spritzes, big tables and a proper Hall Street local crowd.
localTip: Book ahead — it fills fast most nights; if you can't get a table, slip into the sister bar Orazietto next door for pizza and a drink.
tradeOff: It's up on Hall Street with no ocean view, dinner-focused (lunch is weekends only), and priced above a casual beach feed.

name: Etheus
address: Shop 4, Bondi Pavilion, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A fire-led Greek restaurant inside Bondi Pavilion serving shared meze and chargrilled plates a few steps from the sand.
whyGo: One of the beachfront's buzziest recent openings: House Made Hospitality reworked the former Promenade dining room into a fire-and-charcoal Greek room, riding Bondi's Greek wave. We'd choose it for a group dinner of generous shared plates with ocean light, and its share-focused menu makes it an easy pick for feeding a crowd.
bestFor: Group dinners and celebratory shared feasts by the beach
whatToOrder: Lean into the fire and the shared format: pork neck souvlaki, chargrilled meats, meze and dips, spanakorizo, raw tuna with dakos, stuffed peppers, and bougatsa for dessert.
atmosphere: Light-filled, laid-back and lively; fire-driven and unpretentious.
localTip: If you live nearby, come on a Wednesday evening — locals from Bondi, North Bondi, Tamarama, Waverley, Bondi Junction or Bronte get 30% off, plus BYO of one bottle per table with no corkage.
tradeOff: It's a proper restaurant, not a beach snack — shared-plate dining at this level adds up, and it's closed Monday and Tuesday with lunch only on weekends.

name: Lola's Italian & Bar
address: Level 1, 180-186 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A first-floor Italian restaurant and bar overlooking Bondi Beach from Campbell Parade, now trading the venue's original pan-Mediterranean menu for comfort-led pasta, seafood and a serious drinks list.
whyGo: Originally launched in 2021 as Lola's Level 1 by Fratelli Paradiso alumnus Marco Ambrosino and Manny Spinola, the venue has since re-focused as Lola's Italian & Bar, an easygoing pasta parlour with head chef Toby Stansfield (ex-Fabbrica, The Old Fitz) running the kitchen. What sets it apart is the vantage point: a level-one balcony that puts you above the Campbell Parade bustle with a panoramic sweep of the sand and surf, which is a genuinely rare thing on this strip. We'd choose it when you want a proper sit-down Italian meal with a view rather than a casual counter feed, whether that's a long boozy lunch or an intimate dinner.
bestFor: A view-forward Italian lunch or date-night dinner above the beach
whatToOrder: Lean into the Italian comfort core: house-made pasta such as spaghetti with vongole, a cotoletta alla Milanese, freshly shucked oysters from the bar, calamari or fritti, and pane pomodoro with cured meats to start. The wine and cocktail list is a genuine strength, so it is worth a pre-dinner drink on the balcony.
atmosphere: Moody, intimate and design-led, with an easy bar energy that lifts as the evening goes on
localTip: Book a balcony or window table rather than settling for the interior room, and time a weekend visit for the midday opening when the light over the beach is at its best.
tradeOff: It is a first-floor room set back above the promenade rather than directly on the sand, and the drinks-heavy, date-night lean makes it a better fit for couples and groups than for families with young kids.

name: Mapo
summary: A slick, architect-designed gelateria directly opposite Bondi Beach, serving old-school Italian gelato made with no stabilisers or artificial anything.
whyGo: This is the Bondi outpost of Newtown's well-regarded Mapo, and it takes its craft seriously: gelato churned without stabilisers or preservatives, held in traditional lidded pozzetti at a precise -11 to -12 degrees, with the recipes reportedly tweaked for Bondi's saltier, more humid seaside air. The line-up leans classic and single-origin (Sicilian pistachio, Piedmont hazelnut, Bolivian chocolate, fior di latte, Pepe Saya sea-salt caramel) rotated with seasonal fruit sorbets. If you want a genuinely good scoop within sight of the sand rather than a mass-market tub, this is our pick on Campbell Parade.
bestFor: A high-quality post-beach gelato right on the promenade
whatToOrder: The Sicilian pistachio and Piedmont hazelnut are the flavours to test a real gelateria on; single-origin Bolivian chocolate and sea-salt caramel for the classics, or a seasonal fruit sorbet if you want something lighter. Take it in a waffle cone.
atmosphere: Small, design-led shop-front — black track lighting, raw brick and plaster, plywood counters — built for grab-and-go rather than lingering.
localTip: It's directly across the road from the beach and stays open till 10 or 10:30pm, so we'd grab a cone here after dinner and eat it on the promenade rather than queuing at the more touristy spots.
tradeOff: It's a compact takeaway counter with essentially no seating and no beach view from inside — you're meant to take your scoop and walk.

name: North Bondi Fish
summary: A Matt Moran seafood restaurant perched at the quiet north end of Bondi Beach, with arguably the best sand-and-ocean outlook of any dining room on the beach.
whyGo: This is our pick when you want the Bondi beachfront view to do the heavy lifting: it sits right above the sand at the north end, looking straight down the arc of the beach. The kitchen (part of Matt Moran's Solotel group) keeps things coastal and seafood-led — daily sashimi, oysters, whole market fish, fish and chips — in a relaxed, social room that tips into a livelier bar-and-cocktail scene as the day goes on. We'd choose it for a long lunch or sunset drinks over a formal dinner.
bestFor: Long beachfront lunches, oysters and cocktails with a view
whatToOrder: Sydney rock oysters, daily sashimi, whole market fish, fish and chips or a fish burger, and one of the margaritas.
atmosphere: Relaxed, sun-lit and social, getting livelier (DJs, cocktails) into the afternoon and evening.
localTip: Book a table on the outdoor terrace and aim for the golden hour before sunset — the north-end position means the light rakes right across the beach. In winter, note it periodically transforms into "North Bondi Nami," a Japanese izakaya-style pop-up in the same space, so check which menu is running before you go.
tradeOff: You pay a premium for the position — it's pricier and often busier than the fish-and-chips it's named for, and it can get loud once the bar picks up.

name: Raw Bar
summary: A long-running North Bondi sushi bar known for fresh sashimi and its iconic hand rolls, tucked into a corner shop a short walk from the beach's northern end.
whyGo: Raw Bar has been a North Bondi fixture for decades, and it's the place locals send you for properly fresh sushi rather than a sit-down Japanese dinner. We'd choose it for a quick, high-quality lunch or an early dinner grabbed on the way past the beach, with the hand rolls and sashimi doing the heavy lifting. Just know it trades comfort for quality: the space is tiny and it leans heavily on takeaway.
bestFor: A fresh sushi fix straight off the beach
whatToOrder: Hand rolls and sushi cones (temaki), sashimi, and sushi rolls or mixed platters.
atmosphere: Tiny, buzzy, no-frills corner sushi bar.
localTip: Seating is minimal and it's takeaway-focused, so order your cones and eat them across the road on the North Bondi grass or beachfront; come off-peak to dodge the queue.
tradeOff: Cramped with little seating, often a wait at peak times, and on the pricey side for the portion sizes — it's a grab-and-go sushi stop, not a leisurely dinner destination.

name: Shuk
summary: A buzzy Israeli-Mediterranean cafe and bakery on a North Bondi corner, built around family-sized shakshuka, house-baked breads and specialty coffee.
whyGo: This is the original of what's grown into a small Sydney group, and the North Bondi corner site is still where it feels most at home — a former 40-year mixed business turned all-day cafe with breads and pastries baked on-site. The cooking leans Israeli and Mediterranean with modern touches, generous and made for sharing. If you want a Bondi brunch with more character than the beachfront strip, this is a strong pick.
bestFor: Long, shared Israeli-Mediterranean brunch a few blocks back from the sand
whatToOrder: The family-sized shakshuka with fresh bread for dipping is the signature; also look to the house-baked pastries and breads, mezze-style plates (hummus, falafel, pita) and the coffee.
atmosphere: Lively, sociable daytime cafe with outdoor seating on a quiet residential corner
localTip: It's on the corner of Mitchell Street and Murriverie Road, a short walk up from the beach rather than on Campbell Parade — worth the detour, and weekend mornings get busy so aim early or expect a wait.
tradeOff: Daytime only (roughly 6am to mid-afternoon), so it's a breakfast/brunch/lunch spot, not a dinner option.

name: Shuk by the Beach
address: Pacific Bondi Beach, Shop G07/180 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A beachfront outpost of Sydney's SHUK group serving Israeli-inspired falafel, hummus bowls and bakery items grab-and-go style, directly across Campbell Parade from Bondi Beach (it also trades as Shuk Falafel).
whyGo: SHUK is one of Sydney's better-known Israeli kitchens, and this Campbell Parade location puts its falafel wraps, hummus bowls and weekend shakshuka right where you want them, opposite the sand at Pacific Bondi Beach. It began as a pop-up and stuck around as a permanent spot, leaning into a fast, street-food format that suits a beach day rather than a long sit-down. We'd choose this over a big brunch when you want something fresh, vegetable-forward and quick to carry.
bestFor: A quick, fresh Israeli bite straight off the beach
whatToOrder: Falafel or sabich in a pita or wrap, a hummus bowl with pita and pickles, cauliflower shawarma, weekend shakshuka, and house-baked bread and pastries; coffee for the walk.
atmosphere: Casual, lively street-food counter with limited seating, built for takeaway
localTip: Seating is minimal and the format is grab-and-go, so order to take away and eat it across the road on the promenade or the grass above the beach.
tradeOff: It's a quick counter-service spot rather than a sit-down restaurant, so don't come expecting a leisurely table with a view.

name: Makuto
summary: A colourful Hall Street cafe trading specialty coffee alongside Venezuelan arepas and Caribbean pan-tropical plates, a few blocks back from the sand.
whyGo: If you're bored of the usual Bondi smashed-avo circuit, this is where we'd send you: Makuto swaps the beach-cafe template for Venezuelan corn arepas, spiced Caribbean curries and one of the more characterful coffee programs on Hall Street. It opens early (from 6am most days) and pulls a genuinely local crowd around communal tables, with the owner's music taste dialled in as tightly as the espresso. It's a rare thing in Bondi, a cafe with a point of view that isn't just another flat-white-and-bowls operation.
bestFor: An early, flavour-forward breakfast or brunch with a Caribbean twist
whatToOrder: Our pick here is the breakfast arepas and the Caribbean-spiced curries; the coffee is worth ordering on its own merits, and there are vegan and vegetarian options across the menu.
atmosphere: Bright, lively and unpretentious, with communal seating and a strong music sensibility.
localTip: Come before 8am if you want a quiet table and the pick of the arepas; weekend mid-morning brings the full Bondi brunch crush to a fairly compact room.
tradeOff: It's set back on Hall Street, so there are no ocean views and no beachfront seating, this is a destination for the food and coffee, not the outlook.

name: The Crabbe Hole
summary: A tiny, view-blessed coffee window tucked at the pool entrance of Bondi Icebergs, serving strong coffee and simple, well-sourced breakfast and lunch plates.
whyGo: Our pick here is the setting: you order at the counter and grab one of a handful of tables looking straight over the Icebergs pool to the ocean, which is about as good as a coffee view gets in Bondi. The menu is deliberately short but the sourcing is serious — Mothersky Coffee house blend, Brickfields pastries and bread, Pepe Saya butter — so it punches above its cafe-window size. If you're coming straight off the beach or finishing the coastal walk, this is the spot we'd choose for a restorative coffee and a quiet sit.
bestFor: A scenic coffee-and-pastry stop by the Icebergs pool
whatToOrder: A strong flat white or espresso on the Mothersky house blend, a Brickfields pastry with jam and Pepe Saya butter, or the Croque Madame; toasties and seasonal salads round out the lunch end.
atmosphere: Compact, unfussy and view-first — counter service with a few coveted poolside tables.
localTip: Space is genuinely tiny and the pool-facing tables fill fast, so come early on a weekend morning or plan to take your coffee to the promenade; there's indoor seating to duck into if the sea breeze picks up.
tradeOff: It's a small counter cafe, not a sit-down restaurant — limited seating and a short menu mean it's better for a coffee and a light bite than a leisurely group meal.

name: Totti's Bondi
summary: Merivale's buzzy, share-style Italian tucked into the back of The Royal on Bondi Road, built around a wood-fired oven and a leafy, olive-tree-lined courtyard.
whyGo: This is the original Totti's, and it's still the one locals name-check when they want relaxed Italian done properly a short stroll up from the beach. The kitchen (a Merivale project fronted by chef Mike Eggert) leans on a wood-fired oven and a menu made to share, so we'd choose it for a long, unhurried table rather than a quick bite. The big skylit courtyard and pub bones give it energy without the fine-dining formality.
bestFor: Long, shared Italian lunches and lively group dinners off the beach
whatToOrder: The famous wood-fired bread is the non-negotiable order here, ideally alongside the burrata; from there we'd build a table of antipasti (sardines, scallop crudo, marinated peppers), a grilled snack or two, and a couple of pastas to share.
atmosphere: Warm, lively and social, with a sunny Mediterranean-courtyard feel under skylights and olive trees.
localTip: It's on Bondi Road, roughly a kilometre back from the sand rather than beachfront, so book ahead and treat it as a destination sit-down rather than a post-swim walk-up, and angle for a courtyard table on a clear day.
tradeOff: Prices sit at the higher casual end and portions are made for sharing, so it works better for a group than a solo or budget meal; some diners rave about the bread more than the mains.

name: Carbón
summary: A hacienda-inspired Mexican restaurant on Bondi Road where the whole kitchen orbits a woodfire grill, turning out charcoal-kissed tacos, share plates and wagyu steaks.
whyGo: This is the Bondi Road pick when you want Mexican that goes well beyond the usual taco-and-margarita template — Mexico City-born chef-owners cook over a mesquite-fed parrilla, sealing meats, seafood and house-made corn tortillas in wood smoke. The room is an intimate, candlelit space dressed in Mexican textiles, and the drinks list leans into proper mezcal and tequila alongside signature margaritas. We'd choose it for a lively dinner with friends or a date that wants a bit more depth than a quick burrito.
bestFor: Woodfire Mexican for a lively group dinner or a date night
whatToOrder: Start with share plates from the "Para Compartir" section — guacamole and fresh oysters — then build tacos from the house-made corn tortillas (barbacoa and seafood fillings are the signatures). If you're settling in, the wood-fired steaks and slow-roasted meats like suckling pig or lamb shoulder are the reason the grill exists. Order a jalapeño or violeta margarita, or work through the mezcal list.
atmosphere: Intimate, candlelit and buzzy — white walls, dark timber and smoke from the open grill.
localTip: Come on a Tuesday for Taco Tuesday ($5 tacos, $15 margaritas) if you want the food on a budget — but book ahead for weekend dinners and the bottomless brunch, because the 60-odd seats fill fast.
tradeOff: It sits up on Bondi Road rather than by the sand, so there are no ocean views, and it's pitched a notch above cheap-and-cheerful on price.

name: China Diner
address: Level 1, Pacific Building, 180 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A longstanding modern-Cantonese diner that has swapped its old Hall Street room for a first-floor beachfront space on Campbell Parade, trading in steamed dumplings, XO stir-fries and a serious cocktail and sake list.
whyGo: After a decade as a Hall Street favourite, China Diner moved down to the Pacific building overlooking the sand, and the upgrade suits it: moody 1930s-Shanghai styling, an ocean outlook and a kitchen that does contemporary Cantonese with more polish than the "diner" name suggests. We'd choose this when you want a proper sit-down dinner near the beach rather than a quick bite, or for a leisurely Sunday yum cha. The drinks list is a genuine draw, so it works as much for a cocktail-and-dumplings evening as a full meal.
bestFor: A polished modern-Cantonese dinner or Sunday yum cha near the beach
whatToOrder: Our steer is the steamed dumpling selection to start, then the XO king prawns and the twice-cooked crispy chicken; the chicken-and-sesame spring rolls are a signature, and the Sunday yum cha service is the move if you're in on a weekend.
atmosphere: Dim, moody and cocktail-bar-ish at night, brighter and more relaxed for weekend lunch and yum cha.
localTip: Book the weekend lunch or Sunday yum cha sitting if you want the beach view in daylight — the evening service leans dark and loungey, so the ocean outlook is more of a night-time backdrop than the main event.
tradeOff: It sits at the pricier end for the precinct ($$$, mains around the mid-$30s), and the dark, drinks-led evening room is less suited to young kids than the daytime yum cha.

name: North Bondi RSL
summary: A member-and-guest RSL club perched above the northern end of Bondi Beach, serving affordable modern-Australian bistro food with some of the best ocean views in the area.
whyGo: We'd choose this for the view-to-value ratio: a breezy balcony looking straight down the sand, paired with honest club-bistro pricing you won't find anywhere near the beachfront. It's the reliable family option in North Bondi, with generous plates of the pub classics done well, and a lively, no-fuss atmosphere that swings from afternoon-beer casual to a busier buzz on live-music nights. You'll need to sign in as a guest, but that's the only friction.
bestFor: Affordable ocean-view lunch or early dinner with kids or a group
whatToOrder: Our pick here is the club-bistro staples done properly: chicken schnitzel or parmi, a steak on the weekly steak-night special, wood-fired pizzas, and the seasonal seafood plates when they appear.
atmosphere: Relaxed, family-friendly club with a beach-chic edge; livelier on DJ and live-music nights.
localTip: Skip the interior tables and head straight for the balcony seats outside — they're first-come, so arrive a touch before the midday opening or the sunset rush to claim a spot over the water.
tradeOff: It's a licensed club, so non-members need to sign in as a guest, and the food is dependable rather than destination-level.

name: Promenade Bondi Beach
address: Shop 4, Bondi Pavilion, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A multi-venue beachfront complex inside Bondi Pavilion, pairing an all-day contemporary-coastal Beach Bar with Etheus, a smarter Greek dining room, both looking straight out over the sand.
whyGo: Location is the whole pitch here: you're perched on the Pavilion apron directly above Bondi Beach, which almost no other sit-down kitchen in the precinct can claim. The Beach Bar runs a crowd-pleasing coastal menu of oysters, tuna crudo, wood-fired pizzas and seafood mains that works equally for a casual post-swim lunch or a sunset drinks session, while the newer Etheus dining room (opened September 2025 by House Made Hospitality) takes things upmarket with open-flame Greek meze and charcoal-oven plates. We'd come for the setting first and eat to match the occasion.
bestFor: Beachfront lunch, sunset drinks, or a Greek dinner with a view
whatToOrder: At the Beach Bar, our pick leans to the raw and wood-fired end — oysters, tuna crudo, burrata and a share pizza with a seafood main. At Etheus, the meze do the talking: saganaki, tirokafteri and kataifi-wrapped prawns before something off the charcoal oven.
atmosphere: Bright, breezy and lively by day; more polished and date-worthy at Etheus after dark.
localTip: Book the Etheus Verandah or grab a Beach Bar table timed for late afternoon so you're eating as the sun drops behind the Pavilion — the beachfront tables go first, so reserve rather than chancing a walk-in on weekends.
tradeOff: You pay a clear premium for the beachfront position, and the Beach Bar enforces a 90-minute table turn at busy times, so it's not the spot for a long, lingering lunch.

name: Rivareno Gelato Bondi
address: Retail 2/124 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: Authentic Italian gelato made fresh daily on-site, on the busy Campbell Parade corner a short stroll from the sand.
whyGo: This is the Bondi outpost of Rivareno, a Sydney gelato name with a serious following, and their fifth store opened here for the summer season on the corner of Campbell Parade and Hall Street. The gelato is churned each morning in an in-store laboratorio, and the texture is properly dense and velvety rather than aerated. If you rate your gelato, our pick here would be the classic Italian flavours and the sorbets, which locals reliably rank above the bigger chains.
bestFor: A post-beach or after-dinner gelato stop with the family
whatToOrder: Signature Cremino Rivareno, pistachio, and the fruit sorbets; in winter they also do crepes, affogato, hot chocolate and tiramisu.
atmosphere: Bright, busy counter-service gelateria with a handful of seats and constant Campbell Parade foot traffic.
localTip: It stays open late (to around 11pm on weekends), so we'd save it for after dinner when the beachfront queues have thinned rather than fighting the mid-afternoon crush.
tradeOff: It's a busy corner counter, not a sit-down spot, and prices sit a notch above supermarket gelato — you're paying for the fresh-daily quality.

name: Taqiza
summary: A lively Mexican taqueria and agave bar tucked into the Hub on Hall Street, built around a rotating spread of regional tacos, ceviches and margaritas.
whyGo: Run by the Milpa Collective team, Taqiza has been a Bondi fixture for years and reopened as a bigger "2.0" just off the main Hall Street strip after a six-year run on Glenayr Avenue. The kitchen goes well beyond the usual, with a dozen tacos spanning meat, seafood and genuinely good plant-based options alongside shared plates like street corn and quesabirria. With resident DJs on vinyl and Latin bands on Sunday sessions, we'd choose this for a colourful, drinks-forward dinner rather than a quiet meal.
bestFor: A tacos-and-margaritas night out with friends
whatToOrder: Order across the taco board (Baja fish, slow-cooked brisket quesabirria and the vegan chorizo are the signature spread), the tropical guacamole and the tajin street corn to share, washed down with a classic or jalapeno margarita.
atmosphere: Colourful, buzzy and bar-leaning, with blush walls, DJ and live Latin sets on weekends
localTip: Come on Taco Tuesday, when tacos drop to around $6 with cheap Tecates and margaritas, or book the Saturday bottomless brunch if you want the full party version.
tradeOff: It's loud and drinks-driven with no beach view, so it's not the spot for a quiet dinner or a young-family meal.

name: Beach Bar at Promenade Bondi Beach
address: Shop 4, Bondi Pavilion, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: The ocean-facing, walk-in bar terrace inside the restored Bondi Pavilion, pouring cocktails and an all-day coastal menu straight above the sand.
whyGo: This is the drinks-and-a-view arm of Promenade Bondi Beach, House Made Hospitality's big Pavilion revival, and it has one of the best positions on the whole beach — an outdoor terrace looking directly over the sand and water. We'd choose it when you want a proper cocktail and something to graze on without committing to the full Etheus dining room next door, and because the terrace is walk-in only it's the spot to aim for on a spur-of-the-moment sunny afternoon. The all-day kitchen means you're covered whether it's a mid-morning bite or a golden-hour session.
bestFor: Sunset drinks and grazing straight off the beach
whatToOrder: Sydney rock oysters and a cocktail to start, then graze across the wood-fired pizzas, house pastas, or the seafood plates; the shared "For The Table" option is the value pick for a group.
atmosphere: Relaxed and sun-soaked by day, livelier come evening; open-air terrace with prime beach views.
localTip: The terrace is walk-in only, so if you want a front-row table for sunset, come early rather than banking on a booking — reservations run through the Etheus dining room, not the bar.
tradeOff: Pavilion-front position and mid-range pricing mean it's neither cheap nor quiet; tables carry a 90-minute limit at busy times.

name: Gertrude & Alice Cafe Bookstore
summary: A beloved, book-lined Bondi cafe and second-hand bookstore just off Hall Street, serving all-day breakfast, honest lunch plates and its famous chai amid stacks of new and used books.
whyGo: This is one of Bondi's genuine institutions — nearly two decades of shelves crammed floor-to-ceiling with new and second-hand books, tables tucked between them, and a warm, unhurried literary feel you won't find in the beach's polished brunch rooms. We'd choose it when we want somewhere to actually linger: read, work, or nurse a pot of their well-known chai without anyone rushing the table. It's the antidote to Campbell Parade's see-and-be-seen crowd.
bestFor: Lingering with a book, coffee and a slow solo or two-person breakfast
whatToOrder: Our pick is the G&A famous chai served in a pot, alongside a breakfast roll (bacon or the halloumi veggie version) or the avocado smash; leave room for the home-made sweet treats like banana bread.
atmosphere: Cosy, bohemian and quietly literary — books on every surface, low-key and unhurried
localTip: Come on the earlier side of a weekday morning if you want a table to yourself with a book; weekends fill up and the charm is in staying a while, not queuing for it.
tradeOff: It's a block back from the sand with no ocean view, and the busy, browsed-in setting won't suit anyone after a slick, spacious brunch.

name: Harry's Bondi
summary: A beloved North Bondi cafe going strong since 1997, turning out specialty coffee, generous brunch plates and easy-going lunches just back from the sand on Wairoa Avenue.
whyGo: Harry's is one of those Bondi fixtures that has quietly become an institution — it started as a hole-in-the-wall espresso spot in 1997 and grew into a light, airy, blue-and-white room that locals treat as an extension of their kitchen. We'd choose it when you want the real Bondi cafe ritual rather than a beachfront tourist trap: strong coffee, seasonal brunch cooking, and a crowd that's equal parts regulars, families and post-swim visitors. It's a dependable all-rounder that does the classics properly.
bestFor: Weekend brunch and a proper Bondi coffee ritual
whatToOrder: Order the specialty coffee and one of the brunch signatures — the fritters (their feta version is a longstanding favourite), a bircher or the smoothie/matcha line-up; at lunch the kitchen leans into lighter seafood-forward plates like calamari and pasta.
atmosphere: Bright, beachy and buzzy — turquoise accents, indoor and street-side seating, a steady local hum.
localTip: Come early or plan around the weekend rush; if you're a runner, the Friday 6:10am Run Club gets you a discounted coffee or matcha afterwards.
tradeOff: It sits a block back from the sand on Wairoa Avenue, so despite the beachy feel you don't actually get an ocean view — and peak weekend mornings mean a wait.

name: Lox Stock & Barrel
summary: A New York–inspired Jewish deli cafe on Glenayr Avenue turning out house-boiled bagels, cured meats and generous all-day brunch a few blocks back from the sand.
whyGo: This is the corner of Bondi where the cafe crowd goes for something with a bit more character than smashed avo — bagels boiled and baked on site, pastrami and pickles cured in-house, and a menu that leans into proper deli craft. It's a warm, buzzy neighbourhood room that fills fast with locals on weekends, and the "farm-to-plate" kitchen backs up the New York deli theme with real from-scratch cooking. We'd choose it when you want a substantial, characterful brunch rather than a quick beachfront coffee.
bestFor: A hearty, characterful deli-style brunch away from the beachfront crush
whatToOrder: The house-boiled bagels are the signature — chopped liver or house-cured pastrami on rye are the deli classics to reach for, and the vegetable-forward brunch plates (their sprouted-grain bowls and slow-roasted eggplant) cover the lighter end. Pair it with coffee pulled on their lever-piston machine.
atmosphere: Lively, warm and unpretentious neighbourhood deli
localTip: It's up on Glenayr Avenue, not on Campbell Parade, so it stays a notch calmer and more local than the beachfront strip — but weekend mornings still get a queue, so come early or be ready to wait for a table.
tradeOff: Breakfast and lunch only (roughly 7am–2:30pm) — despite some older listings mentioning dinner, the venue currently runs daytime hours, so it's not an evening option. It's also a short walk from the sand rather than a beachfront view.

name: Masala Theory
address: The Hub, 75/79 Hall Street, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A bright, neon-lit "Neo-Indian" restaurant on Hall Street reinventing classic Indian dishes as bold, shareable plates.
whyGo: This is the Bondi outpost of the popular Surry Hills original, and it brings genuinely inventive cooking rather than another curry house — think chicken curry bombs, koliwada prawns and a strawberry chicken curry the kitchen claims you won't find anywhere else. The room leans hard into a playful cyberpunk-meets-jewel-tone aesthetic (hot pink banquettes, neon signs, gold accents), which makes it a natural fit for a lively group dinner. Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options are clearly marked throughout, so mixed-diet tables are easy here.
bestFor: Lively group dinners and celebrations over shared Indian plates
whatToOrder: The signature sharing plates are the draw — chicken curry bombs (a filled panipuri riff, also vegetarian and vegan), the koliwada-battered prawns, and one of the standout mains like the strawberry chicken curry, burnt onion chicken kari or lamb bunny chow served in a hollowed loaf.
atmosphere: Bright, buzzing and colourful — neon, jewel tones and high energy, with indoor seating and a covered outdoor terrace.
localTip: The undercover outdoor terrace is dog-friendly, so it's a rare Bondi dinner option if you've got the dog with you after a beach walk. Book ahead for weekend dinners — the room fills and it leans loud.
tradeOff: It's firmly in the "lively and loud" camp with an energetic fit-out, so it's the wrong pick for a quiet, intimate meal — and there are no ocean views despite the Bondi Beach address.

name: The Bergs Bistro (Bondi Icebergs Club)
summary: The rebuilt club bistro inside Bondi Icebergs, serving honest, seasonal Modern-Australian bistro food across two bars with a full-length view over the famous ocean pool and North Bondi headland.
whyGo: This is the accessible, everyone-welcome counterpart to the fine-dining Icebergs Dining Room upstairs, and after a 2025 renovation it delivers arguably the best value view in Bondi. You get the iconic clifftop pool-and-headland outlook without the white-tablecloth price tag, in a room built for casual lunches, family dinners and post-swim beers. We'd choose it when we want the Icebergs vista but are dressed straight off the sand.
bestFor: A big view on a modest budget
whatToOrder: Our pick is the Bergs' famous battered fish (south-coast bream, house chips, remoulade); otherwise lean into the seasonal bistro staples and pull up at one of the two bars for a drink with the view.
atmosphere: Bright, renovated, casual and lively — a proper members-club bistro perched over the ocean pool.
localTip: Sign in as a guest at reception (bring photo ID) and grab a window or terrace-side table at golden hour — the light coming off the pool and headland is the whole reason to come.
tradeOff: It is a licensed club, so expect ID sign-in, a pokies-and-bar backdrop and food that is dependable bistro fare rather than destination cooking — for that, book the Dining Room upstairs.

name: The Shop & Wine Bar
summary: A long-running back-street cafe on Curlewis Street that pours coffee and comfort food by day and slides into a cosy organic-leaning wine bar by night.
whyGo: This is one of those Bondi locals' rooms that visitors rarely stumble on, tucked a few blocks back from the sand rather than on the tourist strip, and it's built a genuine reputation — a community-voted best wine bar in the eastern suburbs. The kitchen leans into from-scratch comfort food (the house sandwiches, Italian meatballs, hearty salads) while the list runs to organic, skin-contact and preservative-free wines, and the whole place has the feel of a slightly rowdy living room. We'd choose it when we want somewhere that works equally well for a morning flat white and an evening glass without ever feeling like a scene.
bestFor: A relaxed local wine-and-plates evening away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: The signature house sandwiches, Italian meatballs and the seasonal salads by day; by night lean on the organic and skin-contact wines by the glass, and time a visit for the Tuesday or Sunday pasta-and-wine nights.
atmosphere: Warm, snug and neighbourhood-y — a cafe by daylight, a low-lit living-room wine bar after dark.
localTip: Come for the 4–6pm happy hour with $9 selected drinks, or book ahead for the Tuesday and Sunday pasta nights, which fill up with regulars.
tradeOff: It's a couple of streets back from the water, so there are no ocean views and it's a small room that can get tight and loud when it's busy.

name: Wellington Cake Shop
summary: A family-run, old-school Austro-Hungarian cake shop on Bondi Road, baking strudels, tortes and poppy-seed rolls the same way since 1979.
whyGo: This is one of Bondi's genuine time capsules — a tiny Hungarian bakery that has been turning out exquisitely layered continental cakes on the shop-lined stretch of Bondi Road since 1979. We'd choose it when you want something with real heritage rather than another minimalist cafe slice: the cabinet runs from sour-cherry and cheese strudels to dobos torte and a bell-shaped chocolate kuglof. It's a counter-service, cash-and-carry sort of place, so come for the baking, not the ambience.
bestFor: A heritage Hungarian cake fix away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Our pick here is the classic Austro-Hungarian repertoire — dobos torte (layered sponge with chocolate buttercream), sour-cherry and cheese strudel (retes), bejgli poppy-seed roll, and the chocolate kuglof. They also do bagels and everyday bakery items.
atmosphere: Unpretentious, old-world neighbourhood bakery — a display cabinet and a queue, not a sit-down cafe.
localTip: It's on Bondi Road roughly midway between Bondi Junction and the beach, so fold it into the walk or bus ride down rather than expecting to stumble on it beachfront — and go early, as the best cakes and strudels sell through and queues build.
tradeOff: It's a takeaway counter with limited seating and a no-frills, sometimes-brusque service style — you're here for the baking, not a leisurely coffee stop.

name: Fish Shop
summary: An elevated fish-and-chip shop and natural-wine seafood bar from the Fishbowl team, set a block back from the sand on the North Bondi corner of Glenayr Avenue.
whyGo: This is what happens when the people behind Fishbowl decide to do fish and chips properly: a chef-designed room (by George Livissianis) that works equally as a grab-and-go chipper and a sit-down seafood wine bar. The kitchen runs a revolving market-fish list alongside oysters, tartare and Mediterranean-leaning bar snacks, so you can go as light as a dozen rock oysters and a glass of something natural, or as classic as beer-battered fish and chips in paper. It's our pick when you want the Bondi fish-and-chip ritual without settling for a generic tourist fryer.
bestFor: Upmarket fish and chips and a natural-wine seafood graze near the beach
whatToOrder: The fish burger is the signature and the reason many people come back; beyond that, look to whatever's on the market-fish board, the classic fish and chips, oysters and the seafood-and-Mediterranean bar snacks like tartare and anchovy toast.
atmosphere: Bright, coastal and buzzy — half laid-back chipper, half wine bar, spilling toward the adjacent park.
localTip: Order it to take away and walk the two minutes down to the North Bondi end of the sand — the room fills up fast on warm evenings, and the fish burger travels well.
tradeOff: You pay a clear premium over a standard fish-and-chip shop, and it sits a block back from the water, so there are no real ocean views from the tables.

name: Funky Pies
summary: A dedicated all-vegan pie shop and café tucked up on Glenayr Avenue in North Bondi, turning out handmade plant-based savoury pies, sausage rolls and sweet bakes.
whyGo: This is one of the few Bondi spots built entirely around vegan pies, so it does the plant-based version properly rather than as an afterthought. We'd point vegans and the vegan-curious here for a genuinely satisfying pastry-and-coffee stop, with a sustainability streak (biodegradable packaging, plant-based sourcing) that reads as real rather than marketing gloss. It's a neighbourhood pie counter more than a sit-down destination, which is exactly its appeal.
bestFor: A quick, hearty vegan pie fix away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Their handmade savoury vegan pies are the whole point; the vegan sausage rolls and sweet bakes round out a grab-and-go order, with coffee to go alongside.
atmosphere: Casual, no-frills local pie counter
localTip: It sits up on Glenayr Avenue rather than on the Campbell Parade beach strip, so pair it with a walk back down toward the sand and eat your pie on the grass at the north end rather than expecting a view from the shop.
tradeOff: It's a small takeaway-first pie shop, not a place to linger — don't come expecting beach views or a full sit-down café experience.

name: Ikaria Bondi
summary: A lively Greek taverna-style restaurant perched high on Campbell Parade with Bondi Beach views, built around house-made meze, shared plates and Mediterranean spritzes.
whyGo: Named after the Greek "Blue Zone" island, Ikaria leans into long, unhurried island-style dining: pita and house-made dips, saganaki, seafood like kingfish crudo and grilled prawns, all designed to share. It sits elevated across from the sand, so you get the beach outlook without being in the thick of the beachfront crush. With a late kitchen and cheap late-night drinks, it works as both an easy post-beach lunch and a group launchpad for a Bondi night out.
bestFor: Shared Greek plates and spritzes with a beach view
whatToOrder: The house-made pita-and-dip trio (hummus, taramasalata, muhammara), saganaki, and the shareable seafood plates such as calamari and grilled prawns.
atmosphere: Relaxed, sun-washed Mediterranean-island feel — terracotta, clay pots, archways and rattan — that gets lively into the evening.
localTip: Come for the happy hour window from 5pm for discounted spritzes and pita with dips, or roll in after 10pm when margaritas drop to a flat cheap price — a rare late, affordable option this close to the sand.
tradeOff: It's a meze-and-drinks share format that skews toward evenings and groups, so it's less suited to a quiet, sit-down solo meal or young families after bedtime.

name: Little-L Chicken & Burgers
summary: Long-running North Bondi chicken-burger specialist on Campbell Parade doing grilled and fried chicken burgers, wraps, wings and loaded fries for around $15 a plate.
whyGo: This is one of North Bondi's genuine old-timers, flipping chicken burgers since 2007. We'd choose it for a proper feed at a fair price over a designed-for-Instagram burger, and the loyalty in its reviews shows it delivers consistently.
bestFor: A cheap, reliable post-beach chicken-burger feed
whatToOrder: Their reason-for-being is the chicken burgers (grilled or fried) — the Ben Buckler is the one locals name, and there are wraps for a lighter option plus wings and loaded fries to round it out.
atmosphere: Casual, unpretentious takeaway shopfront
localTip: Order ahead on the app or by phone at peak times — it's a small kitchen and the counter gets a queue on warm evenings when everyone's drifting up from the beach.
tradeOff: It's a workaday takeaway counter, not a sit-down destination — you're here for the burger, not the view or the room.

name: Rocker
summary: A buzzy all-day Mediterranean bar-and-diner at the northern end of Campbell Parade, from Darren Robertson (Three Blue Ducks) and Stuart Toon.
whyGo: Rocker does that versatile Bondi thing well: light-timber dining room and a proper cocktail bar under one roof, with a produce-driven Mediterranean menu that shifts from focaccia-and-snacks brunches into house-made pastas and feasting plates by night. The founders' pedigree shows in the cooking, and the drinks program (margaritas shaken every which way, a wide wine list) means it works equally as a long lunch or a late session. We'd choose this when you want somewhere that can flex from a relaxed midday bite to a lively dinner without changing venues.
bestFor: Bottomless brunch, group dinners and drinks-led all-day sessions
whatToOrder: House-baked focaccia with confit garlic butter to start, then the house-made pastas (ox-cheek pappardelle is a signature) or a shared feasting plate; the Sunday roast is the standout weekend order, and there's a well-regarded vegan roast alternative.
atmosphere: Light, airy timber dining room paired with a lively cocktail bar; relaxed by day, buzzier with music by night.
localTip: Our pick is a Sunday: the roast is genuinely one of Bondi's better ones and the room settles into an easy afternoon session, but book ahead because that's when it fills fastest.
tradeOff: Closed Mondays, and being a popular spot on busy Campbell Parade it gets loud and crowded at peak times, so it's not the pick for a quiet, intimate dinner.

name: Society Pizza e Pesce
summary: A buzzy Curlewis Street pizzeria-and-bar from the Faro family that pairs Neapolitan wood-fired pizza with a Southern Italian, robata-grilled seafood menu just up the hill from the sand.
whyGo: This is the Society group's clever "e Pesce" (and seafood) extension of their well-loved Bondi pizza bar, built around the idea that Bondi was short on great seafood. The kitchen runs a robata-style charcoal grill for skewers and whole plates alongside a proper Neapolitan pizza oven, so a table can split blistered pizza and Sicilian-dressed seafood in one sitting. We'd choose it when you want something more considered than a quick slice but still relaxed, loud and beach-adjacent rather than fussy.
bestFor: A lively Italian sit-down mixing pizza and grilled seafood near the beach
whatToOrder: Our pick is one from each side of the kitchen: a wood-fired pizza (the diavola and prawn-and-chilli are signatures) plus something off the charcoal robata grill — Yamba prawns, or tuna and salmon skewers with Sicilian salmoriglio. The slow-poached octopus carpaccio is a known starter, and cocktails are taken seriously.
atmosphere: Bright, lively room built around an open kitchen and pizza oven, with playful Sicilian hand-gesture artwork on the walls.
localTip: Weekdays it opens for dinner only (from around 5pm), but on Saturday and Sunday it runs all day from noon — so it's your daytime option here if you're coming straight off the beach for a long weekend lunch.
tradeOff: It's a block back on Curlewis Street rather than on the promenade, so come for the food and buzz, not for ocean views.

name: Anita Gelato
summary: A world-travelling boutique gelato chain's Bondi Beach outpost, churning 150-odd handmade flavours a few steps from the promenade.
whyGo: This is the Israel-born Anita Gelato's Campbell Parade shopfront, sitting almost opposite the sand and beside QT Bondi, so it's the natural full-stop on a beach walk or a warm evening on the strip. The draw is sheer range — well over a hundred rotating flavours spanning classic gelato, dairy-free sorbets, frozen yoghurt and soy- and sugar-free options — plus a wall of toppings, sauces and jams you can pile on. It stays open late, making it one of the more reliable after-dinner sweet stops on this side of Bondi.
bestFor: A late post-beach or after-dinner gelato with the whole family
whatToOrder: Signature gelato flavours like Madagascar vanilla, pistachio or espresso; the dairy-free fruit sorbets if you want something lighter; and don't skip loading on the house toppings and sauces.
atmosphere: Bright, busy walk-up counter with a holiday-strip buzz
localTip: Grab your cup or cone to go and cross to the promenade or grass above the sand — the shop itself is a counter, not a place to linger, and the beach is the better seat.
tradeOff: It's a polished international chain rather than a homegrown Bondi original, and the premium handmade product is priced accordingly — locals loyal to Gelato Messina may not be swayed.

name: Besa
summary: A lively Spanish tapas bar on Hall Street from the ESCA/Aalia group, pouring Basque- and Madrid-inspired share plates, seafood and cocktails a couple of blocks back from the sand.
whyGo: This is Bondi's polished take on a Spanish tapas bar, from the team behind Aalia, Nour and Henrietta, with executive chef Ibrahim Kasif (ex-Porteno, Bodega, Stanbuli) running a produce-driven kitchen of croquetas, crudo, tinned seafood and Basque-style fish. The 65-seat room is moody and mid-century with a wine-led list and Don Quixote-inspired cocktails, and it flexes easily between a proper dinner and a drop-in drink. We'd choose this when we want the energy of a tapas bar rather than a beachfront view.
bestFor: Share-plate dinners and cocktails with a group or a date
whatToOrder: Lean into the "picoteo" tinned seafood (anchovies, razor clams, house-pickled sardines and mussels), the croquetas and crudo, a Basque-style seafood dish such as John Dory with pil pil, and finish with Basque cheesecake or churros.
atmosphere: Moody, mid-century and buzzy, with Spanish-leaning funk and house on rotation.
localTip: It's on Hall Street in the Bondi Beach hub rather than on the beachfront, so come for the food and vibe, not a sea view — and the midday-open Saturday and Sunday sittings (including a bottomless lunch) are the easiest way in.
tradeOff: No ocean outlook and a mid-to-upper price point once share plates and drinks add up; it's a dinner-and-drinks bar rather than a family or kid-focused spot.

name: Chaco Ramen Bondi
summary: A buzzy, Fukuoka-inspired ramen and izakaya spot just off Hall Street, the Bondi sequel to Keita Abe's cult Chaco Bar and Chaco Ramen on Crown Street.
whyGo: This is where you come when you want ramen with genuine pedigree rather than a tourist-strip bowl.
bestFor: A satisfying, well-made ramen dinner with a drink, close to the beach
whatToOrder: Our steer is a signature bowl — the creative chilli-coriander or yuzu-scallop ramen, or a classic chicken-soy if you want it straight — plus the Bondi-only plates like John Dory dumplings, prawn fried rice or taro chips, and a round of grilled skewers to share. Ask for kaedama (extra noodles) if you're still hungry.
atmosphere: Lively, casual and convivial, with a street-stall feel and a hand-painted mural anchoring the room.
localTip: Book ahead through OpenTable for dinner — it's a compact, popular room and walk-ins can wait; lunch service runs Friday to Sunday if you'd rather a quieter midday bowl, and takeaway is available via the Bopple app.
tradeOff: It's a sit-down izakaya-priced experience rather than a cheap quick feed, and it's set back from the beachfront with no ocean view — come for the food, not the scenery.

name: Drake Eatery
address: 178A Curlewis Street (corner of Curlewis & Gould Streets), Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A Bondi local's Modern Australian spot from chef Ian Oakes, working as a relaxed cafe by day and a candle-lit, produce-driven restaurant with a proper wine bar by night.
whyGo: This is one of those neighbourhood restaurants Bondi locals quietly guard: a short, seasonal Modern Australian menu built around sustainable produce, cooked with real technique rather than beach-town shortcuts. The corner room is warm and unfussy — recycled timber, low light, a bar you can perch at with a glass of boutique local wine — and it flexes from a daytime coffee-and-plate to a considered dinner. A block back from the QT Bondi lobby, it's the kind of place we'd choose when we want the beach nearby but a grown-up meal that isn't fighting the crowds on Campbell Parade.
bestFor: An unhurried, grown-up dinner or a leisurely wine at the bar, a block off the sand.
whatToOrder: Look to the signatures: the pan-seared gnocchi with mushrooms, hazelnuts and blue cheese that's been on the menu since day one, the roast duck Oakes is known for, and the line-caught fish of the day; finish with the ricotta doughnuts or the honeycomb-and-white-chocolate parfait.
atmosphere: Warm, low-lit and unpretentious — recycled timber and copper, with a convivial wine bar up front.
localTip: Bookings are sensible for dinner (they take reservations via Resy or email), but if you're solo or a two, the bar seats are the move — perch there for a glass of local wine and a couple of small plates without needing a table.
tradeOff: Set back from the promenade on the Curlewis/Gould corner, so there's no ocean view — this is about the food and the room, not the water.

name: Easy Tiger
summary: A loud, colourful Southeast Asian street-food diner and cocktail bar on Campbell Parade, with an ex-Mr Wong chef and its own Bondi Brewing Co microbrewery on site.
whyGo: This is where we'd send a hungry group that wants a bit of a party with dinner: chef Andrianto Wirya (ex-Mr Wong, Queen Chow) roams across Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Singapore and the Philippines with fun, snackable riffs, and the choose-your-own banquet takes the guesswork out of feeding a crowd. The on-site Bondi Brewing tanks and a proper cocktail list mean the drinks keep pace with the food. Our pick for a lively, shareable meal a block back from the sand rather than a quiet, view-first dinner.
bestFor: Group dinners and long, shared banquets near the beach
whatToOrder: Go for the signature snacks — beef rendang party pies, twice-fried crispy corn larb and the Balinese suckling-pig bao — then a laksa-spun char kway teow or claypot Hainanese chicken rice; the choose-your-own banquet is the easy move for a table, washed down with a house Bondi Brewing beer or a South Bondi Tiger cocktail.
atmosphere: Lively and loud — rattan, big lanterns, long communal tables and a busy cocktail bar
localTip: Book one of the communal or outdoor terrazzo high tables ahead on weekends, and keep an eye out for their midweek "bottomless baos" deal if you're after a low-key Wednesday feed.
tradeOff: The room runs loud and the all-Australian wine list can bite — it's a fun, buzzy diner rather than a quiet or beachfront-view dinner, and it sits across the road from the sand, not on it.

name: Fishbowl
address: 180 Campbell Parade, The Pacific Bondi, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: The original Fishbowl, a build-your-own poke and fresh-salad bar on Campbell Parade that kicked off Bondi's poke craze back in 2016.
whyGo: This is where the Fishbowl chain started, and it's still the one we'd point people to when they want something fresh, fast and genuinely good straight after the beach. You build your own bowl from a base of cabbage, brown rice or glass noodles, add raw salmon, tuna, kingfish or tofu, then load up on pickled ginger, herbs, seaweed, a dressing and a crunchy element. It's quick, customisable and light enough that you don't feel weighed down for the rest of the day.
bestFor: A fast, fresh, customisable lunch off the beach
whatToOrder: A build-your-own poke bowl — salmon or tuna over brown rice with ginger, seaweed and a crunchy topping; the tofu base makes it an easy vegan pick.
atmosphere: Bright, busy, order-at-the-counter fast-casual; mostly grab-and-go
localTip: Order ahead on the Fishbowl app or website to skip the lunchtime queue, then eat it on the grass at the south end of the beach a two-minute walk away.
tradeOff: It's counter-service takeaway with limited seating, so it's for a quick bowl rather than a sit-down meal.

name: RND (Raw Next Door)
address: Shop 2, 136 Wairoa Avenue, North Bondi NSW 2026
summary: A moody seaside Japanese izakaya that materialises three nights a week inside North Bondi's Harry's cafe once the roller door comes down after dark.
whyGo: This is the after-dark alter ego of beloved daytime cafe Harry's, reimagined by the crew behind the Raw Bar (one of eastern Sydney's original Japanese restaurants, going since 1995) with chef Jack New of Edition Coffee Roasters and Izy Izakaya pedigree. The menu leans into premium sashimi, robata-grilled skewers and share plates built on heat, smoke and restraint, served under Japanese films projected onto exposed brick. We'd choose it for a low-lit, grown-up dinner that feels a world away from Bondi's daytime bustle.
bestFor: A moody, grown-up izakaya dinner with sake and share plates
whatToOrder: Premium sashimi and Hokkaido scallops, robata skewers ("things on sticks") like burnt-honey chicken and miso oyster mushrooms, the lobster tempura sando, and a mochi bomb to finish.
atmosphere: Dim, sultry and intimate — moody lighting, projected old Japanese films on brick, a shelf of sake.
localTip: RND only runs Friday to Sunday evenings from around 5.30pm, so don't turn up on a weekday expecting izakaya — that same address is just Harry's cafe by day. Book ahead for a weekend table.
tradeOff: Limited to three nights a week and it's an elevated, small-plates format, so costs add up and it won't suit anyone after a casual weeknight feed.

name: Anita Gelato (Bondi Beach)
summary: A buzzy, Tel Aviv-born gelateria on Campbell Parade churning 150-plus handmade flavours a stroll from the sand.
whyGo: This is the Bondi Beach outpost of Anita's globe-spanning gelato brand, and it earns its queue: everything is made on site, the flavour wall runs deep, and the sauce-and-topping theatre makes it a genuine treat for kids. If you're coming straight off the sand and want a cold hit with more range than the average scoop shop, we'd choose this on the strip.
bestFor: A post-beach dessert stroll along the promenade
whatToOrder: A two-scoop cup or cone mixing a nut-based classic (pistachio, hazelnut) with a fruit sorbet; ask about the halva and Middle-Eastern-leaning flavours that set Anita apart, and the frozen yoghurt if you want it lighter.
atmosphere: Bright, busy, family-friendly counter service with a lively queue on warm evenings
localTip: The line looks long but moves fast, and the staff are happy to let you taste before you commit, so don't be shy about sampling one of the off-beat flavours before ordering. Come on the earlier side of the evening if you want a quieter counter.
tradeOff: It's a premium global chain rather than a hidden local secret, prices sit above a basic scoop, and seating is minimal, so this is really a takeaway-and-walk spot.

name: El Indio Bondi Beach
summary: A lively, casual Colombian street-food spot at the North Bondi end of Campbell Parade, built around hand-shaped corn arepas and generous rice-and-beans bowls.
whyGo: El Indio does one thing and does it with real conviction: gluten-free white-corn arepas stuffed with slow-cooked meats, plantain, black beans and guacamole, alongside build-your-own corrientazo bowls that come out seriously generous. It's a warm, informal neighbourhood room rather than a view restaurant, and the kitchen is unusually kind to vegetarian and vegan diners, so a mixed table rarely has to compromise. We'd choose it when we want punchy, flavour-forward Latin food a short walk from the sand without a big-night budget.
bestFor: Casual Latin American dinners and a relaxed happy hour with friends
whatToOrder: Our pick is the arepas — the Bondi Pavillion (beef brisket, plantain, black beans, chimichurri) on the meat side and the vegan Ghandi (eggplant, plantain, black beans, guacamole, hogao) — plus a corrientazo bowl to share; finish with the dulce de leche cheesecake, and time a margarita for happy hour.
atmosphere: Warm, informal and lively, with a handful of street-facing outdoor tables.
localTip: Come for the 4–6pm happy hour on arepas and cocktails; if you're arriving for dinner Wednesday to Friday, book ahead because the small room fills fast, though tables turn over quickly.
tradeOff: Limited trading days and hours (typically closed Monday–Tuesday, dinner-led) and a compact, casual space — this is a quick, cheerful feed, not a leisurely ocean-view sit-down.

name: Glory Days
address: Bondi Pavilion, Shop 3, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A licensed, beachfront all-day diner inside the restored Bondi Pavilion, serving California-leaning breakfast and lunch with a direct sightline to the surf.
whyGo: Its position is the whole pitch: umbrella-shaded patio seats look straight out over Bondi Beach, and the sun-washed terracotta-and-timber fit-out leans into the Pavilion's Spanish architecture. The menu is confident all-day café cooking with a Californian accent rather than standard smashed-avo fare, and being licensed means you can slide from a morning coffee into an oyster-and-a-glass lunch without changing tables. We'd choose this when the view matters as much as the plate and you want a sit-down brunch right on the sand's edge.
bestFor: A beachfront sit-down brunch or lunch with an ocean view
whatToOrder: Our pick leans to the signatures: the loaded breakfast burrito, the vegetable-forward Goodness Bowl, and at lunch the club chicken sandwich, oysters or the lamb ragu pappardelle. There's also a takeaway coffee window pouring Stitch Coffee if you're just passing.
atmosphere: Bright, breezy and beach-facing; buzzy at weekend brunch, more relaxed on a weekday morning.
localTip: The takeaway window means you don't have to commit to a table — grab a Stitch coffee to go and walk it along the promenade if the patio has a weekend queue.
tradeOff: You're paying a beachfront-Pavilion premium, and reviews flag that service and consistency can wobble when it's slammed — go early if you want the calm version.

name: Iberica
summary: A Balearic-inspired Spanish tapas and wine bar on the quieter, locals' end of Bondi Road, from the team behind neighbouring Ikaria.
whyGo: This is the grown-up, date-night side of Bondi's Spanish scene: an intimate room of curved archways and warm Mediterranean styling that channels small towns on Ibiza and Mallorca rather than the beachfront bustle. The kitchen, led by an executive chef with a serious Spanish-cooking pedigree (Porteño, Bastardo), turns out shareable tapas and generous paellas alongside a genuinely Spanish-focused wine list and a proper cocktail program. We'd choose it for a lingering, wine-led dinner up on Bondi Road when you want atmosphere over a view.
bestFor: Couples and small groups after a wine-led Spanish tapas dinner
whatToOrder: Order to the room's strength: the seafood paella de marisco (there's a green vegetable paella too), grilled octopus with smoked potato cream, salted cod croquettes, house bread with truffle butter, and churros with dulce de leche ice cream to finish.
atmosphere: Intimate, buzzy and softly-lit, with an Ibiza-meets-Mallorca warmth
localTip: It only opens from dinner most nights (Wednesday to Sunday), with lunch added on Saturday from noon, so it's an evening plan rather than a post-beach lunch stop — and being up on Bondi Road, it's an easy walk from the sand but well away from the Campbell Parade crowds. Book ahead, as the room is small.
tradeOff: No ocean view and limited daytime hours; this is a Bondi Road dinner destination, not a beachfront or all-day spot.

name: Macelleria Bondi
address: G09/180 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A part-butcher, part-steakhouse on Campbell Parade where you pick your cut from the glass counter and watch it cook on the open grill.
whyGo: We'd choose this for a no-fuss steak or burger when you've come straight off the sand and want quality meat without the fine-dining ceremony. It works as a genuine hybrid — a working butcher counter up front, a casual grill and dining room behind it — so you can either sit down or buy cuts to cook yourself. The choose-your-own-cut theatre and grass-fed, dry-aged focus give it more character than the usual beachside burger stop.
bestFor: A casual steak or burger straight off the beach
whatToOrder: Grass-fed Angus and dry-aged steaks picked from the counter, flame-grilled beef burgers, or the butcher's sausages and skewers; a veggie burger and halloumi salad cover the non-meat crowd.
atmosphere: Laid-back and busy, with open-grill and butcher-counter energy.
localTip: It doesn't take bookings, so at peak beach hours expect to wait — or skip the queue entirely and buy cuts, sausages or skewers from the butcher counter to grill back at your place.
tradeOff: Walk-ins only means peak times can mean a wait, and while it's steps from the sand it sits across Campbell Parade rather than on a true beachfront terrace; the premium aged and wagyu cuts climb well past the casual burger price.

name: Makaveli Bondi
address: Shop 2/179 Glenayr Avenue, North Bondi NSW 2026
summary: A pocket-sized, day-to-night contemporary eatery on Glenayr Avenue that pours Will & Co coffee from early morning and swaps to cocktails and Italian-leaning small plates by night.
whyGo: This is the kind of tucked-away neighbourhood spot we'd steer people toward when they want the real Bondi rather than the beachfront crowd. It runs two lives in one 28-seat room: an easy morning cafe for coffee and pastries, then a lamplit little bar trading in bright Mediterranean small plates and genuinely good cocktails. The cooking punches above the size of the space, and the room shifts convincingly from daytime casual to evening intimate.
bestFor: A relaxed evening of small plates and cocktails away from the beachfront bustle.
whatToOrder: Lean into the small plates built for sharing — burrata and greens, charred broccolini, ricotta with roasted grapes, and the taleggio croquettes — and pair with one of the house cocktails or a glass from the independent-leaning wine list. Coffee and focaccia if you're calling in during the morning shift.
atmosphere: Small space with a big personality; textured, muted interiors that dim into something warm and intimate at night.
localTip: It's genuinely tiny (28 seats) — book ahead through OpenTable for an evening table, or come at the 6am–midday cafe end when you can usually just walk in for a coffee.
tradeOff: No beach or ocean views and it's a side-street nook, so come for the food, drinks and vibe rather than a view — and the small-plates-and-cocktails format isn't the cheapest way to fill up.

name: Rorouni
address: Shop 2A, 71–77 Oxford Street, Bondi Junction NSW 2022
summary: A tiny 18-seat Bondi Junction kaisen counter where ex-Josh Niland chef Tom Tse turns dry-aged fish into precise, build-your-own seafood rice bowls.
whyGo: This is one of the more interesting Japanese openings to land near the beach in 2026, and the reason to go is the fish itself: chef Tom Tse honed his craft under Josh Niland and brings that dry-aging obsession to a tight, deliberate donburi menu. We'd choose this when we want something considered rather than casual — an 18-seat room built around a single idea done carefully, with dry-aged bluefin at its centre. It's a short walk from the Bondi Junction interchange, which makes it an easy, grown-up detour before or after the beach.
bestFor: A considered solo or couples' seafood lunch near the interchange
whatToOrder: The kaisendon is the signature — a build-your-own bowl over koshihikari rice with dry-aged bluefin tuna (akami, otoro and mince); look also to the aged-fish donburi and blistered mackerel with the crisp-fried sides.
atmosphere: Intimate, counter-focused and deliberate — an 18-seat room built around the fish.
localTip: With only 18 seats and a chef pedigree that draws a crowd, treat this as a book-ahead or off-peak spot rather than a walk-in — and come for lunch when the dry-aged bowls are the whole point.
tradeOff: It's a narrow, single-minded menu in a very small room — go for the dry-aged donburi, not for variety, groups or kids.

name: Sefa Kitchen
summary: A lively, share-plate Middle Eastern and Mediterranean restaurant on Bondi Road built around Levantine meze, fire-cooked meats and communal platters.
whyGo: This is the Bondi Road spot we'd choose when a group wants to eat with their hands and linger over a spread rather than order neatly per person. The kitchen leans into Levantine and broader Mediterranean traditions — house dips, chargrilled skewers, slow-roasted lamb and fire-led vegetables — and there's a genuine occasion energy to it, from cheese-wheel pasta nights to weekend Egyptian-style brunch. It's more of a destination dinner than a beach pit-stop, so it rewards a booking and an appetite for sharing.
bestFor: Group dinners and celebratory shared feasts
whatToOrder: Order across the table: the meze section (hummus, baba ganoush, popcorn olives, lamb kofta and grilled prawn skewers), at least one from-the-fire centrepiece like the 24-hour slow-roasted lamb shoulder or the market fish, a pasta such as the harissa prawn or lamb pappardelle, and baklava to finish.
atmosphere: Warm, communal and buzzy — big platters, shared tables and a licensed bar with cocktails.
localTip: Come on a Wednesday or Thursday to take advantage of BYO nights (standard corkage) and pair it with a bottle from a nearby Bondi Road bottle shop; weekends are for the bottomless Mediterranean lunch and Egyptian-style brunch, so book ahead for those.
tradeOff: It's a set-back-from-the-sand Bondi Road restaurant with no ocean view, dinner-focused and priced for a proper sit-down feast rather than a quick post-swim bite.

name: Brown Sugar Bondi
summary: A long-standing, intimate BYO Mediterranean bistro a block back from the sand on Curlewis Street, serving seasonal Italian- and French-leaning plates since 1995.
whyGo: This is one of Bondi's genuine old-timers — a small, candlelit neighbourhood bistro that has quietly outlasted most of the beachfront's churn since 1995. We'd choose it when we want a proper sit-down dinner with warm, personal service rather than a scene, and the BYO policy makes it one of the better-value ways to have a special meal near the beach. The kitchen leans Mediterranean, with Italian and French influences over local seasonal produce.
bestFor: A relaxed, romantic BYO dinner away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Seasonal Mediterranean plates and the house fish pie it's long been known for; the weekend Sunday roast if you're in mid-afternoon.
atmosphere: Intimate, warm and unhurried — a small dining room plus a newer al fresco area.
localTip: It's BYO, so bring your own bottle and save on the markup — grab wine from a nearby Bondi bottle shop on the way. The room is small, so book ahead via SevenRooms rather than risk a walk-in.
tradeOff: It's set back on Curlewis Street with no ocean view, and the room is small, so it's about the food and intimacy rather than the beach scene.

name: Gelbison Pizzeria Ristorante Italiano
summary: A no-frills, family-run southern Italian pizzeria and ristorante that has been feeding Bondi a block back from the beach since 1987.
whyGo: This is one of the last of the old-guard Bondi Italians, a family operation that has stuck to honest pizza and pasta for nearly four decades while the rest of Campbell Parade reinvented itself. We'd choose it for a loud, warm, unpretentious dinner where the room is full of locals and regulars rather than a tasting-menu crowd. It's BYO-friendly and generous with portions, which makes it a genuinely good-value option in an increasingly expensive precinct.
bestFor: A relaxed, BYO family or group dinner off the beach
whatToOrder: Our steer here is the wood-style pizzas (the Calabrese has a following), the build-your-own pasta where you pair the shape with the sauce, the Zuppa di Cozze mussels as a starter, and tiramisu to finish.
atmosphere: Buzzy, loud and cheerfully old-school — a proper neighbourhood trattoria that runs on energy.
localTip: It's BYO for a small corkage per head, so grab a bottle from a nearby bottle shop before you sit — and book ahead, because the room fills fast on weekends.
tradeOff: Dinner only (from 5pm) and service can slow right down when it's packed, so it's not the spot if you're in a hurry or want a lunchtime table.

name: Porch & Parlour
summary: A proudly female-owned, independent all-day cafe tucked on Ramsgate Avenue at the quieter North Bondi end, doing produce-led brunch a short stroll from the sand.
