whyGo: This is the North Bondi neighbourhood cafe we'd point you to when you want a proper sit-down brunch away from the Campbell Parade crush. The kitchen leans seasonal and vegetable-forward, with in-house baking and a menu that's unusually generous to vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free eaters. It suits a relaxed morning where you're happy to settle in rather than grab and run.
bestFor: A settled-in, produce-led North Bondi brunch
whatToOrder: The green pea pancake with avocado, whipped feta and egg is the signature; also look to the ricotta pancakes, the Middle Eastern bowl, and the range of one-hander sandwiches and burgers for something heartier.
atmosphere: Laid-back and light, with Mediterranean-influenced distressed walls, tilework and an outdoor area.
localTip: It's at the calmer Ramsgate Avenue end of North Bondi rather than on the main beachfront strip, so come here when the Campbell Parade cafes are packed out — and note the kitchen skews toward daytime, with a short summer sunset window on top of the core morning hours.
tradeOff: It's a block back from the water, so despite the North Bondi setting you're not getting a full beachfront ocean-view table.

name: Savion on the Grill
summary: A long-running, family-run kosher Israeli grill a block back from the north end of the beach, turning out handmade falafel, fresh pita and generous shawarma plates at cheap-eats prices.
whyGo: Savion is the kind of unpretentious, home-kitchen Israeli joint that's become genuinely rare in Bondi, and it's been doing it on Wairoa Avenue for years. The falafel and pita are made by hand rather than pumped out of a machine, the salads and toppings pile up generously, and you'll pay very little for a properly filling meal. If you want authentic Middle Eastern food without the beachfront markup, this is our pick in North Bondi.
bestFor: Cheap, filling kosher Israeli lunch near the beach
whatToOrder: Handmade falafel plates, lamb or chicken shawarma, hummus with fresh pita, and chicken schnitzel — loaded up with the salad and pickle toppings.
atmosphere: Casual, warm and homey — closer to eating in someone's kitchen than a polished restaurant.
localTip: It's cash only and keeps daytime hours (roughly 10am–6pm), and like a proper kosher kitchen it closes for Shabbat — shut Saturdays and winding down early Friday afternoon, so plan a weekday or Sunday visit and bring notes.
tradeOff: Cash-only, daytime-only trading and a no-frills fit-out mean it's a lunch-run rather than a sit-down dinner destination.

name: Shuk Bakery
summary: An Israeli-style neighbourhood bakery and takeaway from the Shuk group, turning out house-baked sourdough, pastries, bourekas and made-on-site sandwiches a couple of blocks back from North Bondi beach.
whyGo: This is the bakery workshop behind Shuk's popular North Bondi cafe, and it's where we'd send you for the morning-run essentials: proper sourdough, croissants, challah and Israeli-style savouries like flaky bourekas rather than a sit-down brunch. It's a small, functional shopfront built for grabbing and going, with baskets of bread lining the wall and a short list of salads and sandwiches assembled on site. If you want table service and shakshuka you head to Shuk proper down the road; if you want the baking at its source, you come here.
bestFor: Morning bakery runs and takeaway lunch near the beach
whatToOrder: Bourekas, house-baked sourdough and pastries, croissants and challah, plus the made-to-order baguettes and salads; they also carry vegan pastries and gluten-free bread.
atmosphere: Small, busy, grab-and-go bakery shopfront
localTip: It's a working bakery with limited seating, so treat it as takeaway — grab your bourekas and coffee and walk the two blocks down to the sand rather than expecting a table.
tradeOff: Tiny footprint and minimal seating mean it's not the spot for a leisurely sit-down brunch — that's what the larger Shuk cafe nearby is for.

name: Speedos Cafe
summary: A famously photogenic, health-leaning brunch cafe perched above the sand at the north end of Bondi, known for vivid smoothie bowls and all-day breakfast with ocean views.
whyGo: Speedos has built a global reputation as one of the most Instagrammable cafes anywhere, and the draw is real: a bright beachside room looking out over the North Bondi waves, plus a sprawling menu that swings from classic big breakfasts to raw, vegan and gluten-free plates. We'd choose it when you want the postcard Bondi brunch experience with a view, rather than a quiet local hideaway. It leans as much on colour and setting as on the cooking, but for a first-timer wanting the beach-and-bowl shot, it delivers.
bestFor: A photogenic beachside brunch with ocean views
whatToOrder: Our pick is the signature pink pitaya (dragonfruit) bowl or a green smoothie bowl; the caramelised banana pancakes, eggs benedict with smoked salmon, and the Protein Power egg-white plate are the crowd favourites.
atmosphere: Bright, buzzy and colourful, packed with beachgoers and photo-takers, with prized window seats over the water.
localTip: Come early — it opens not long after dawn, and the window and view seats fill fast once the mid-morning brunch crowd arrives, especially on weekends.
tradeOff: It trades on looks and location: tables are tight when it's busy, and some visitors feel the styled dishes run pricey for what lands on the plate.

name: Bennett St Dairy
address: 73 Bondi Road, Bondi NSW 2026 (corner of Bennett Street and Bondi Road)
summary: A bright corner cafe on Bondi Road that pours specialty coffee and does farm-to-table brunch by day, then flips to a relaxed neighbourhood wine bar on Thursday to Saturday evenings.
whyGo: This is a proper locals' cafe up the hill from the sand, the kind of spot people build their weekend around rather than stumble into off the beach. The kitchen leans into seasonal produce and creative brunch plates alongside serious coffee and house-baked cookies and focaccia. What sets it apart is the double life: from Thursday it stays open into the evening as a wine bar with artisan cheese, charcuterie, house-made wagyu biltong and simple share plates, so you can treat it as a morning ritual or a low-key night out.
bestFor: A relaxed local brunch or an early evening wine and cheese away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Lean on the seasonal brunch plates and bowls with your coffee, and don't skip the house-baked cookies or focaccia; in the evening, our pick is the cheese and charcuterie board with the house-made wagyu biltong and a glass off the wine list.
atmosphere: Bright, airy and effortlessly cool by day; warm and low-key as a wine bar after dark.
localTip: It sits on the corner of Bennett Street and Bondi Road rather than down at the beach, so it's an easy, quieter stop if you're staying along Bondi Road or want brunch without the campervan-park scrum near the sand. The wine bar only runs Thursday to Saturday from early evening, so plan an evening visit around those nights.
tradeOff: No ocean views and a short walk from the beach, and the wine-bar service is limited to Thursday through Saturday evenings.

name: Oh'Brian Café
summary: A warm little French-leaning coffee-and-bakery cafe on a quiet Bondi backstreet, doing locally-baked baguettes, pastries and breakfast rolls until early afternoon.
whyGo: We'd choose this for a proper morning coffee-and-pastry stop a block back from the beach crowds, where the baguettes are baked on-site and the French-bakery leaning shows in the pastries and brioche rolls. It's built a genuinely loyal local following (the kind of place people come back to for their long black and a brownie), and it earns points for coeliacs with a dedicated gluten-free cabinet and separate-cook accommodations. Our read: a neighbourhood cafe that does the small things right rather than a destination brunch scene.
bestFor: An early coffee, pastry or breakfast roll off the main drag
whatToOrder: Locally-baked baguettes and French pastries, a bacon-on-brioche breakfast roll, the gluten-free arepas from the coeliac cabinet, and a long black or espresso-based coffee.
atmosphere: Cosy, relaxed neighbourhood cafe with a few outdoor tables and a friendly local vibe.
localTip: It's a mornings-only operation — the kitchen and coffee wind down around 1–1:30pm, so make it a breakfast or early-lunch plan rather than an afternoon one. Coeliacs should ask about the separate gluten-free cabinet.
tradeOff: No ocean views and it's a short walk in from the sand, plus it closes in the early afternoon — not the spot for a long, late brunch or a beachfront seat.

name: Pompei's
summary: A long-running, family-run Italian trattoria a block back from the sand on Roscoe Street, best known for wood-fired pizza and its own house-made gelato.
whyGo: Pompei's has been a Bondi fixture since 1999, and it earns its longevity by doing simple things properly: honest Italian cooking, a genuinely good wood-fired pizza, and gelato churned on site that locals rate among the best in the area. It's the kind of unfussy, dependable neighbourhood spot we'd steer people to when they want a real meal over a beach-club scene, with a street-front gelato window that pulls a steady after-beach crowd. Casual, lively and licensed (no BYO), it works equally for a family dinner or a low-key date.
bestFor: Casual family pizza dinners and after-beach gelato
whatToOrder: A classic margherita or one of the wood-fired pizzas, followed by a scoop or glass of the house gelato — hazelnut is the flavour Pompei's is most known for.
atmosphere: Relaxed, buzzy and family-friendly
localTip: You don't have to sit down to enjoy the best-known thing here — the street-front gelato stand lets you grab a cone to walk back down to the beach, which is our pick on a hot afternoon.
tradeOff: It's a block back from Campbell Parade, so there are no ocean views — you're coming here for the food and the gelato, not the outlook.

name: The Corner House
summary: A long-running corner restaurant on Bondi Road serving rustic wood-fired pizzas, house-made pasta and Mediterranean share plates, with an intimate cocktail bar and balcony upstairs.
whyGo: This is one of those neighbourhood fixtures that has quietly anchored the Denham Street corner of Bondi Road for over a decade, occupying a heritage building that was once a Bondi tram stop. Downstairs is easygoing and pizza-led; upstairs turns into a cosy cocktail bar with a sprawling balcony that suits a longer night or a group booking. We'd choose it when you want a reliable, unfussy Italian feed away from the beachfront crowds rather than a scene.
bestFor: A relaxed local Italian dinner or a group celebration up the hill from the beach
whatToOrder: Wood-fired pizzas are the signature here (the loaded meat-heavy options get the most love), backed by house-made pasta and Mediterranean-style share plates; the pasta can be made gluten-free on request.
atmosphere: Warm and lively downstairs, cosier and bar-focused upstairs with a balcony
localTip: Head upstairs to the cocktail bar and balcony if you want the quieter, more intimate side of the venue — it's the better call for couples or a drawn-out evening than the busier ground floor.
tradeOff: It's a good ten-minute walk up Bondi Road from the sand with no ocean view, and reviewers note the pizzas run a touch pricey for the style.

name: The One That Got Away
summary: A Bondi Road stalwart since 1996 that works as both a fresh fishmonger and a fish-and-chips takeaway, plus in-house seafood cooking with an Asian-inflected slant.
whyGo: This is one of the genuine Bondi Road institutions — owner Barry Rallis has been running it for nearly three decades and still does the early-morning Sydney Fish Market run himself. It's more than a chip shop: alongside proper battered fish and chips there's a wet fishmonger counter and cooked dishes that stray happily into grilled and Asian-influenced territory. We'd choose this when you want dinner sorted without a sit-down restaurant — either a takeaway parcel or raw fish to cook at home.
bestFor: A locals' fish-and-chips run or grabbing fresh seafood to cook at home
whatToOrder: Classic battered fish and chips is the anchor; look also to the grilled and marinated fish (think chilli-lemongrass barramundi), salads and the raw/fishmonger selection if you're cooking at home.
atmosphere: Unpretentious neighbourhood seafood shop, more counter-and-collect than dining room.
localTip: Our tip: it doubles as a fishmonger, so you can buy fillets to cook yourself rather than only ordering fried — handy for a self-catered night near the beach. It's a short walk up Bondi Road from the sand, not on Campbell Parade.
tradeOff: It's up Bondi Road rather than beachfront, and it's a takeaway/counter operation — no view or table service to speak of.

name: Trattoria Elva
summary: A neighbourhood Italian trattoria and natural-wine bar up on Bondi Road, making fresh pasta by hand every day.
whyGo: This is the kind of low-key, properly Italian spot locals keep to themselves rather than the beachfront crowd-pleasers down the hill. The kitchen leans on handmade pasta and classic Roman technique, backed by a thoughtful list of Italian and natural wines and a short menu of bar snacks and cocktails. We'd choose it for an unhurried weeknight dinner when you want real cooking over a view.
bestFor: An unhurried, grown-up Italian dinner away from the beach
whatToOrder: Whatever the daily handmade pasta is, plus the carbonara (guanciale, egg, pecorino, black pepper) it's known for; the beef cheek risotto is a regular favourite, and a board of salumi and cheese pairs well with the natural-wine list.
atmosphere: Cosy, warm and neighbourhood-scale, with bar seating and a proper wine-bar feel.
localTip: Weeknights each carry a rotating special — think risotto Monday, pasta Tuesday, carbonara Wednesday, steak tagliata Thursday — often around $33–$38 with a matched wine, so mid-week is where the value sits. Saturday lunch runs by request only, so call ahead if you want a daytime table.
tradeOff: The menu is deliberately short and vegetarian choices are limited, and it's a walk up from the beach rather than a between-swims option.

name: Bar Pho
summary: A relaxed North Bondi neighbourhood Vietnamese spot on Warners Avenue built around some of the better pho in the eastern suburbs, plus rice paper rolls, salads and small bites.
whyGo: This is the kind of unfussy, family-recipe Vietnamese kitchen we'd steer you to when you want a warming, well-priced meal a few blocks back from the sand rather than a scene. The pho is the reason to come — clear, aromatic broth done properly — and the menu clearly flags vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free options, so mixed groups are easy to feed. It's a genuine locals' room, quietly consistent and welcoming rather than trend-driven.
bestFor: An easy, good-value Vietnamese dinner away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Pho is the signature — the Hanoi-style chicken pho is a regular pick; round it out with chicken-and-prawn spring rolls, rice paper rolls, or one of the gluten-free vermicelli salads, and there's a well-regarded vegan pho for plant-based diners.
atmosphere: Small, lively and friendly; casual coastal neighbourhood room
localTip: It's a compact room a five-minute walk up from North Bondi Beach, so if you're coming straight off the sand it's an easy detour — and the Square online-ordering page makes it a reliable takeaway option to eat back at the beach or your apartment.
tradeOff: No ocean views and it's set back from the beachfront, and the space is small, so at peak times expect it to fill quickly.

name: Bondi Trattoria
summary: A long-running modern-Italian trattoria on Campbell Parade, directly opposite Bondi Beach, serving classic-with-a-twist pasta and seafood indoors or on the ocean-facing terrace.
whyGo: Trading since 1987, the Trat is one of the beachfront strip's genuine survivors — an old-school neighbourhood Italian that has outlasted a parade of trend-driven openings around it. We'd choose it when you want a relaxed, unfussy sit-down feed of pasta and seafood with a proper view across Campbell Parade to the water, rather than a scene. It's the kind of dependable, all-comers spot that works equally for a family lunch, a casual date, or a group off the sand.
bestFor: A relaxed, dependable Italian sit-down opposite the beach
whatToOrder: Lean into the pasta and seafood side of the menu — house pastas, seafood plates like local bugs, and classic Italian mains are the trattoria's stock-in-trade.
atmosphere: Relaxed, slightly old-school, and lively, with indoor tables and a sought-after ocean-facing terrace.
localTip: Book the terrace via OpenTable if you want the beach view — the outdoor tables go first, especially at weekend lunch when the strip is busiest.
tradeOff: It trades on location and consistency rather than cutting-edge cooking, and prime beachfront positioning means you pay a little more than at a back-street Italian.

name: Cali Press
summary: A long-running Hall Street health cafe built around 100% raw cold-pressed juices, superfood smoothies and wholefood bowls, just up from the sand.
whyGo: This is one of Bondi's original clean-eating institutions, and it still does the genre better than most of the newer arrivals. The kitchen leans plant-forward and wholefood, with a menu that's largely gluten-free and generous with vegan options, paired with AllPress espresso for anyone who wants an actual coffee alongside their green juice. We'd choose it when you want food that's genuinely nourishing rather than beige "healthy" theatre.
bestFor: A post-swim clean breakfast, juice run or grab-and-go wholefood lunch
whatToOrder: Cold-pressed juices and superfood smoothies are the signatures; the warm grain and veg bowls, acai bowls, and tamari tofu sourdough sandwiches are the food picks, plus tonics and elixirs if you're doing a cleanse.
atmosphere: Compact, bright and casual, with a coffee-bar counter and a couple of outdoor tables
localTip: If you're coming straight off the beach, grab a large glass-bottle juice to take away rather than eating in, as seating is limited and turns over fast in the morning rush.
tradeOff: It's a small footprint with only a handful of seats, so it's more a quick-fuel and takeaway spot than a place to linger over a long brunch.

name: Pocket Bondi
summary: An all-day café, bar and Modern Australian restaurant on Campbell Parade that runs from sunrise coffee straight through to late-night cocktails opposite the beach.
whyGo: We'd choose Pocket for its versatility: it's the rare Bondi spot you can drop into for a morning flat white, a casual lunch, or a buzzy dinner-and-drinks without changing venues. The kitchen leans Modern Australian with crowd-pleasing plates and a proper cocktail list, and there's a genuine local-hangout energy rather than a tourist-trap feel. Midweek deals like Wednesday burger night and Tuesday steak night make it easy on the wallet for what's a prime beachfront position.
bestFor: Casual all-day eating and sunset drinks across from the sand
whatToOrder: The PKT cheeseburger is the signature (especially on Wednesday burger night); other regulars point to the raw kingfish, beef tartare, chimichurri sirloin and the miso-glazed eggplant, with a Sunday roast and tiramisu rounding out the menu. Groups of eight-plus can opt for the shared set menu.
atmosphere: Buzzy, friendly and compact — lively and social, especially at sunset and on deal nights.
localTip: Come for the early shift — coffee and breakfast from 6am is a calmer, sunnier way to enjoy the beachfront position before the evening crowd fills the small room.
tradeOff: The space is small, so it gets noisy and tight during peak evening service — not the pick for a quiet, intimate dinner.

name: Surfish Bondi Beach
address: Shop 1, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A family-run, beachfront seafood cafe planted right on the Bondi promenade, serving fish and chips, seafood platters and all-day breakfast with the sand a few steps away.
whyGo: This is one of the few genuinely beachfront tables on the Bondi strip, sitting on Queen Elizabeth Drive with seating that looks straight out over the sand and surf. It has been family-owned since 2005 and keeps things unpretentious: order seafood done simply and well, from fish and chips to a shared platter, without the fine-dining price tag most beachfront views command. We'd choose this when the view and the location matter as much as the food.
bestFor: An easy beachfront seafood lunch straight off the sand
whatToOrder: Fish and chips or calamari for the classic beach feed, the seafood platter to share, or the crab scramble and other cooked breakfasts if you arrive early.
atmosphere: Relaxed, casual and beach-facing, with an open-air feel and a quieter rear courtyard.
localTip: It opens early (from around 6.15am) so it's a strong pick for a post-swim breakfast before the beach crowds build; the front seats with the beach view fill first, so grab one early.
tradeOff: Hours are weather-dependent given the exposed beachfront position, and it's counter-style casual dining rather than a full-service restaurant.

name: Will & Co HQ Tasting Bar
address: Level 1, Shop 7, 184 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026 (corner of Beach Road and Gould Street)
summary: The Bondi headquarters and tasting bar of local specialty micro-roaster Will & Co, where a dedicated brew bar pours single-origin pour-overs, batch brew and cold-brew flights a block back from the beach.
whyGo: Will & Co grew out of three Bondi mates roasting coffee in 2013, and this HQ is where they show what the beans can really do — a hybrid of café, roastery, concept store and barista training studio rather than a full breakfast spot. Our pick here is the Brew Bar: bottomless batch brew, V60 pour-overs across rotating single origins, and tasting flights that let you compare beans side by side, backed by pastries from Tuga. If you take your coffee seriously, this is the most considered cup in the immediate beach precinct.
bestFor: Coffee lovers who want a proper single-origin brew, not just a beachfront flat white
whatToOrder: A V60 pour-over of the day's single origin or a batch-brew tasting flight; the oat-milk cold brew on tap or a gelato coffee shake in warmer weather; a Tuga pastry alongside
atmosphere: Light, calm and design-led — roller doors open to natural light, greenery, ocean-blue and timber tones, local art and low ambient music
localTip: Check the days before you plan around it — it keeps roaster's hours rather than café hours, closed Monday and Tuesday and winding down by early afternoon, so treat it as a morning-to-lunchtime stop.
tradeOff: It's a coffee-first tasting bar and retail space, not a sit-down brunch kitchen — expect pastries rather than a full food menu, and short trading hours.

name: Blackwood Bondi
summary: An all-day Bondi bistro and aperitivo bar on Glenayr Avenue, pairing Mediterranean-leaning brunch plates with a Friday-to-Sunday dinner and cocktails.
whyGo: Blackwood works the whole day from one address a few streets back from the sand: a genuine sit-down brunch of eggs, bowls and sandwiches in the mornings, then a proper evening menu of grilled fish, veal cotoletta and spatchcock come the weekend. Chef Rob Lechowicz brings a serious French-trained pedigree to what could easily have been just another beach cafe, and the aperitivo-and-cocktail side (drinks program tied to the Maybe Sammy team) gives it a grown-up second gear most all-day rooms don't have. We'd choose this when we want somewhere that can flex from a laptop-friendly late breakfast to an actual dinner without changing postcode.
bestFor: All-day brunch that graduates into a weekend dinner and Aperol o'clock
whatToOrder: For daytime, the big breakfast plate or one of the loaded bowls; at dinner, lean into the aperitivo snacks (oysters, prosciutto, cheese) and the grilled mains like snapper or the crumbed veal cotoletta.
atmosphere: Calm, contemporary room in soft greens and greys that lifts into a livelier aperitivo buzz on weekend evenings.
localTip: The dinner service only runs Friday to Sunday evenings, so if you're picturing cocktails and cotoletta, aim for the back half of the week; midweek is a daytime-only affair.
tradeOff: It's a backstreet address on Glenayr, not a beachfront table, so come for the food and the room rather than an ocean view.

name: Bondi Boulangerie
summary: A French artisan bakery and patisserie on Hall Street, a couple of blocks back from the sand, turning out croissants, pastries, breads, sandwiches and coffee daily.
whyGo: This is the kind of no-fuss French bakery Bondi does well: proper laminated pastry, freshly baked baguettes and a counter of quiche and sandwiches that makes it an easy grab-and-go on the walk to the beach. The croissants and pain au chocolat draw the most consistent praise, and the room itself is warm and unpretentious rather than a scene. It is part of a small Sydney group (with Surry Hills and CBD siblings), but the Hall Street shopfront reads as a genuine neighbourhood bakery.
bestFor: A morning pastry-and-coffee run before the beach.
whatToOrder: Our pick here leans to the viennoiserie: the almond croissant and pain au chocolat, a plain butter croissant to judge the lamination, and a slice of quiche with coffee if you want something more filling. Baguettes and sandwiches are the practical takeaway option.
atmosphere: Cosy, warm-lit and casual; a bakery counter rather than a sit-down cafe.
localTip: If you're coming straight off the beach, grab pastries here to take across to the sand rather than fighting for a table at the busier campervan-parade cafes; go earlier in the morning while the viennoiserie is at its freshest.
tradeOff: It's a bake-counter, not a full-service breakfast cafe, and it closes early (around midday-to-mid-afternoon), so it suits mornings far better than a leisurely late brunch.

name: Chapter One Café & Wine Room
summary: A long-running all-day cafe on the Campbell Parade strip serving modern-Australian brunch with an Asian lean, plus specialty coffee and a wine offering, a short stroll from the sand.
whyGo: This is one of the more grounded, genuinely local cafes on the busy Campbell Parade beachfront run, trading since 2011 and leaning on fresh, seasonal produce rather than gimmicks. We'd choose it for an unhurried weekday breakfast when the flashier beach cafes are heaving, and the "& Wine Room" side gives it a bit more range than the average brunch spot. It sits right on the beach strip near Sir Thomas Mitchell Road, so you can roll off the sand and into a table without much of a walk.
bestFor: An easy all-day brunch on the beach strip
whatToOrder: Our steer is the vegetarian brekkie roll it's long been known for, alongside the seasonal salads and wholesome grain bowls; pair it with the specialty coffee.
atmosphere: Relaxed, local, indoor-outdoor cafe seating on Campbell Parade
localTip: It opens early (from 6am), so if you're coming straight off a morning swim you can beat the mid-morning brunch crowd and still get an outdoor table facing the strip.
tradeOff: It's across Campbell Parade from the sand rather than directly beachfront, so views are of the strip rather than an unbroken ocean outlook.

name: Lulu
summary: A polished, pink-hued Pan-Asian bar and restaurant on Hall Street from the long-standing Raw Bar team, serving Japanese-anchored small plates, sushi and shared mains from post-beach spritzes through to late-night dinners.
whyGo: Lulu is Raw Bar's more playful sibling, taking the 30-year Bondi sushi pedigree and pushing it across Korea, Thailand, Vietnam and China with heat and personality. Executive chef Shintaro Honda (ex-Raw Bar) and head chef Bryan O'Callaghan build a menu made for sharing, from crisp Hokkaido prawn-and-scallop toast to wagyu with sansho pepper, in a warm golden room with plush pink walls and a marble bar. We'd choose this for a lively group dinner or a date night that stretches later than planned, backed by proper cocktails rather than a rushed beachfront turnover.
bestFor: Group dinners and date nights with cocktails
whatToOrder: Our pick is the signature Hokkaido prawn-and-scallop toast, plus the Lulu fried chicken and something off the raw/sushi side (nigiri, sashimi or a spicy salmon roll) that nods to the Raw Bar heritage; wagyu with sansho and Peking chicken anchor the larger shared plates, and the miso caramel monaka is the dessert to finish on.
atmosphere: Warm, lively and polished — a golden, pink-walled room with marble bar and banquette seating.
localTip: It's on Hall Street rather than the beachfront, so come for the food and drinks rather than a view — and it leans into the neighbourhood with weekday deals like $2 gyoza nights and weekend bottomless brunch, worth checking their socials before you book.
tradeOff: No ocean views and a share-plate format that adds up quickly — this is a mid-to-upper spend night out, not a cheap post-swim bite.

name: Mamis Bondi
summary: A cobalt-blue, family-run Mexican cantina on Bondi Road serving street tacos, birria and carnitas with nothing over $20 and a fully BYO policy.
whyGo: Run by Mexican-born couple Erendira and Juan Perez in the old Laurie's Vegetarian space, this is homey, unfussy Mexican cooking rather than a slick taqueria concept. We'd choose it for a cheap, cheerful, low-key feed off the beach: everything is priced under $20, it's fully BYO (with a discount deal at the bottle-o across the road), and the room is stacked with board games and family photos. It's the antithesis of the see-and-be-seen Bondi dinner.
bestFor: Budget-friendly BYO family and group dinners
whatToOrder: Street tacos done as a mix-and-match set — the pork confit carnitas and the birria beef with consommé are the house signatures — plus quesadillas and nachos to share.
atmosphere: Bright, casual and family-friendly; shared tables, board games and a homey Frida-Kahlo-blue fit-out.
localTip: Grab your drinks first at The Royal Hotel bottle shop across the road — diners get a discount, and the whole place is BYO.
tradeOff: It's up on Bondi Road well back from the sand, so there are no ocean views and it leans casual over polished.

name: Mojos Tapas Bar
summary: A budget-friendly Spanish tapas bar on Campbell Parade with cushioned sofas and ocean views straight across to Bondi Beach.
whyGo: We'd choose this for an easy, sun-warmed session of small plates and cocktails without leaving the beachfront strip. It leans Spanish tapas with the odd Asian-fusion twist, and the real draw is the setting: sofa seating that looks out over the sand, house sangria, and a lively, unfussy crowd. It's more about the vibe and the view than fine-dining precision, which is exactly what suits a lazy Bondi afternoon.
bestFor: Beachfront tapas, sangria and cocktails with a group
whatToOrder: Shared tapas plates, paella-style and vegetable dishes, a jug of the house sangria, and cocktails; the weekend brunch is worth a look if you're there earlier.
atmosphere: Relaxed, lively and beach-facing, with the noise of the surf and Campbell Parade drifting in
localTip: Aim for a sofa spot facing the water and arrive before the afternoon crowd builds; note the kitchen typically rests Monday and Tuesday, so plan a Wednesday-to-Sunday visit.
tradeOff: It's a see-and-be-seen beachfront bar rather than a destination for serious, authentic Spanish cooking, and the busy Campbell Parade frontage means it can get loud.

name: The Depot
summary: A long-running family-run Bondi cafe on Warners Avenue doing all-day breakfast, bistro-style lunches and an in-house bakery, with a small Wednesday-to-Friday dinner service.
whyGo: The Depot has been a genuine local fixture since 2008, and the cooking leans on seasonal produce and its own bakery rather than the see-and-be-seen theatre of the Campbell Parade strip. We'd choose it for an unhurried weekday breakfast or brunch away from the tourist crush, and it's one of the few neighbourhood cafes here that also flips into a proper sit-down bistro dinner later in the week. It reads as a place locals actually return to, not a one-visit photo stop.
bestFor: Relaxed local breakfast and brunch, plus a low-key midweek dinner
whatToOrder: All-day breakfast plates and cafe classics like a halloumi stack or eggs benedict, the in-house bakery goods, and the well-regarded coffee; they're also known for gluten-free pancakes.
atmosphere: Warm, unpretentious neighbourhood cafe; busy but not frantic
localTip: It sits a couple of blocks back from the sand on Warners Avenue, so it stays calmer than the beachfront cafes on a busy morning — worth the short walk if you want a table without the wait. Note the dinner service only runs Wednesday to Friday, so book ahead for evenings.
tradeOff: Off the beachfront with no ocean views, so it's a food-and-coffee destination rather than a spot for a sea outlook.

name: % Arabica
address: Corner of Hall Street and Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: The Kyoto-born specialty coffee brand % Arabica's first Australian flagship, on the landmark Hall Street and Campbell Parade corner in the heart of Bondi Beach.
whyGo: % Arabica arrives in Bondi as a genuine event for coffee people: a globally minimalist, design-led roaster known for direct-trade single-origin beans, Slayer espresso machines and a pared-back aesthetic that lets the coffee do the talking. We'd choose this for a considered flat white or one of the brand's signature milk drinks rather than a sit-down feed, and its position on the busy Hall Street corner, a short walk up from the sand, makes it an easy stop on the way to or from the beach. It's a marquee opening in a precinct already thick with cafes, so expect a queue and a scene in the early days.
bestFor: A design-led specialty coffee on the way to or from the beach
whatToOrder: The house espresso and flat white are the obvious anchors; % Arabica is also known internationally for its Spanish Latte and Kyoto Latte, plus iced coffee and matcha for the walk-down-to-the-sand crowd.
atmosphere: Minimalist, calm and pared-back; grab-and-go energy on a busy corner.
localTip: This is a coffee-forward roaster, not a brunch kitchen, so pair it with a proper meal elsewhere on Hall Street and treat % Arabica as the coffee stop. As a brand-new flagship, check its live listing for current hours before making a special trip.
tradeOff: Premium pricing and a coffee-and-pastry focus rather than a full food menu, and as a just-opened flagship expect crowds and settling-in teething.

name: Field to Fork
address: LG07/75 Hall Street, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A family-run butcher, deli and gourmet providore in The Hub on Hall Street, selling grass-fed meats, house-made South African biltong and ready-to-eat homestyle meals to take away.
whyGo: This is the Bondi spot we'd point locals to when they want a proper butcher and a providore under one roof rather than a sit-down meal. Alongside the full display of grass-fed steaks, roasts and house-made sausages, they turn out prepared food you can carry home — slow-roasted lamb shoulders, farmhouse roast chickens, lasagna and fresh sandwiches — plus a three-generation line of in-house South African biltong, droewors and boerewors. Our pick here is treating it as your self-catering headquarters for a beach apartment or a picnic on the sand.
bestFor: Self-catering, picnics and quality meat for a home-cooked dinner
whatToOrder: House-made biltong and droewors, the grass-fed steaks and roasts, and prepared meals like slow-roasted lamb shoulder, roast chicken or a fresh made-to-order sandwich.
atmosphere: Bustling, no-fuss butcher-and-deli counter inside the Hall Street Hub food precinct.
localTip: If you're staying in a Bondi apartment or heading for a picnic, grab a roast chicken and some sides here rather than eating out — and pick up biltong for a high-protein beach snack.
tradeOff: It's a takeaway providore and butcher, not a restaurant — there's no dining room, table service or beach view, so it suits stocking up rather than a sit-down meal.

name: Myoko Sushi Bar
summary: A long-running, unfussy Japanese sushi bar one street back from the beachfront, turning out fresh nigiri, sashimi and rolls at neighbourhood prices.
whyGo: This is the kind of steady, dark-wood-panelled local sushi spot that regulars quietly rely on rather than the tourist-facing crowd on Campbell Parade. Open since 2012 and seven days a week, it keeps the format simple: fresh-made nigiri, sashimi, hand rolls, bentos and a handful of cooked mains, done consistently and priced reasonably. We'd choose it when you want a reliable Japanese feed without the queue or the fuss.
bestFor: A dependable, well-priced sushi dinner or bento away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Fresh nigiri and sashimi, hand rolls and a bento box; among the cooked options, gyoza, soft-shell crab salad and chicken katsu round out the menu.
atmosphere: Small, relaxed and minimalist, with dark wooden panelling
localTip: Our pick is to grab it as takeaway or delivery via their online ordering and eat it down at the beach — the dining room is compact and this is a locals' pick-up spot as much as a sit-down one.
tradeOff: It's a functional neighbourhood sushi bar one street back from the sand — no ocean views and no scene, so look elsewhere if you want a destination dining experience.

name: Sabbaba
summary: A cheap-and-cheerful Israeli falafel joint on the Campbell Parade beachfront strip, turning out stuffed pita pockets, plates and bowls to a mostly-vegetarian crowd.
whyGo: Sabbaba is one of Bondi's long-running budget falafel counters, and it's the kind of place we'd point you to when you want a fast, filling, plant-forward feed without a sit-down commitment. The menu leans hard into chickpea-and-tahini territory — flavoured falafel balls, generous pita pockets, salad-loaded plates and bowls, plus dips and hot chips — and almost everything can be built vegetarian or vegan. Now on Campbell Parade after years at its old Hall Street home, it stays open late, which makes it a reliable after-beach or post-swim refuel.
bestFor: A quick, affordable vegetarian/vegan feed near the sand
whatToOrder: A stuffed falafel pita pocket or a falafel plate/bowl loaded with salads and hummus; add a side of hot chips (cooked without animal fats).
atmosphere: Casual, no-frills, order-at-the-counter and go — busy and lively at peak beach hours.
localTip: It's takeaway-first with limited seating, so our move is to grab a pita pocket and eat it across the road on the grass or the promenade rather than hovering for a table.
tradeOff: This is fast, functional falafel rather than a destination meal — don't come expecting a proper sit-down dining experience or an ocean-view fit-out.

name: The TinPin Bakery
summary: A long-running, family-owned artisan bakery and coffee spot on Bondi Road, turning out sourdough, croissants and pastries from early morning.
whyGo: This is the un-flashy, midway-up-Bondi-Road bakery that locals lean on rather than the beachfront tourist queues, baking its own breads and pastries daily and roasting its own coffee. It opens early and keeps things simple and consistent, which is exactly why the neighbourhood keeps coming back. If you want a genuine morning-bakery routine away from Campbell Parade, this is our pick.
bestFor: An early coffee-and-pastry run away from the beachfront crowds.
whatToOrder: Croissants (the almond and chocolate-almond are the ones regulars single out), Danishes and savoury pastries, sourdough and their signature walnut loaf, paired with their house-roasted coffee.
atmosphere: Small, cosy, unpretentious neighbourhood bakery-cafe.
localTip: It opens around 5am, so it's a reliable option well before the Campbell Parade cafes get going. Grab pastries to take down the hill to the beach.
tradeOff: It's a bakery on Bondi Road, not a sit-down beachfront cafe. No views and limited seating. Come for takeaway, not a leisurely brunch.

name: Up South Bondi
summary: A busy neighbourhood brunch cafe midway up Bondi Road, known as much for its photogenic flavoured matcha lattes as for its generous all-day breakfast plates.
whyGo: This is the kind of local cafe we'd point you to when you want the real Bondi Road weekday rhythm rather than a beachfront queue — running since 2018, it's built a genuine community following and a big social-media profile off its colourful matcha program and hearty brunch. The kitchen leans into crowd-pleasing modern-Australian brunch with a strong plant-based streak, so a table of mixed eaters is easy to feed. It's compact and gets loud when it fills, which is part of its charm rather than a knock against it.
bestFor: A relaxed weekday brunch or matcha fix away from the beachfront crush
whatToOrder: Our pick is one of the signature flavoured matcha lattes (pistachio and strawberry are the ones people come for), paired with a brunch plate — the corn fritters, cookie croissant, halloumi tapioca bites or a bacon and egg roll; the vegan big breakfast and vegan shakshuka are the standouts on the plant-based side.
atmosphere: Compact, lively and cheerful; fills up and gets buzzy by late morning.
localTip: Come before midday on a weekday if you actually want a seat — the narrow room packs out fast, and it's an easy takeaway grab if you'd rather walk your coffee down toward the beach.
tradeOff: It's a small, often-crowded space with no ocean outlook, and the specialty matcha drinks sit at a premium price for what's essentially a casual cafe.

name: Yo-Chi Bondi Beach
address: Shop 13, 180 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A self-serve frozen yoghurt and açaí shop on Campbell Parade where you build your own bowl from a wall of soft-serve flavours and a 30-plus topping bar, priced by weight.
whyGo: Yo-Chi landed on Campbell Parade in mid-2024, right beside Anita gelato, and it's become the default post-beach or after-dinner sweet stop for the strip. The draw is control: you pull your own swirls of probiotic froyo (including coconut- and almond-based vegan flavours) and pile on fruit, compotes, mochi, popping pearls and sauces, so a fussy kids' table and a health-leaning adult can both walk out happy. We'd choose this over a sit-down dessert when the group can't agree and everyone wants something slightly different.
bestFor: Customisable froyo for families, groups and late beach-strip cravings
whatToOrder: Build-your-own frozen yoghurt or an açaí base; the signature tart yoghurt is the house benchmark, and the dairy-free coconut/açaí flavours cover vegan and dairy-free eaters.
atmosphere: Bright, casual, self-serve and buzzy — queues build on warm summer evenings.
localTip: It's pay-by-weight, so a bowl that looks modest can climb fast once you load the toppings bar — go easy on the heavy sauces and fruit compotes if you're watching the cost. It's open late (to around 10:30–11pm), making it one of the more reliable after-dinner options on the Parade.
tradeOff: It's a national chain rather than a one-off Bondi original, and there's no ocean view despite being a block from the sand — this is a grab-and-stroll treat, not a destination sit-down.

name: Amalfi Bondi Beach
address: 1 Sir Thomas Mitchell Rd, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A modern Italian restaurant and bar a block back from the sand on Sir Thomas Mitchell Road, built around shared antipasti, house-made pasta and an Amalfi Coast "la dolce vita" mood.
whyGo: If you want a relaxed Italian dinner without fighting for a Campbell Parade window table, this sits just off the main drag with a warm, styled interior and outdoor seating. The kitchen leans into homemade pasta and shared plates, and the format flexes from a couples' date night to a bigger group spread. Recent diners consistently single out the pasta and the attentive service.
bestFor: A casual sit-down Italian dinner a short walk from the beach
whatToOrder: Lean into the pasta e secondi — house pasta like pappardelle con ragù, gnocchi and the saffron prawn ravioli — alongside antipasti to share (burrata, arancini, cured meats) and the wagyu steak tartare.
atmosphere: Warm, styled and lively; can get loud when full
localTip: Locals with a 2026 postcode get 20 percent off on Thursdays, and Wednesday runs a pasta-and-vino deal — worth timing a visit around if you're staying nearby.
tradeOff: It's a block back from the water, so there are no real ocean views, and a few reviewers have flagged it as noisy on busy nights.

name: Chuck Trailer's
address: Shop 7, 152 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A scruffy American-style dive bar just off the Bondi strip, pairing $1 wings and smash burgers with 100-plus bourbons and boilermakers.
whyGo: From the team behind Neighbourhood, this is the anti-Bondi Bondi bar: corrugated cattle-shed roofing over the bar, rock 'n' roll posters and a deliberately thrown-together dive aesthetic that feels more inner-west than beachfront. The draw is cheap wings across a long list of sauces and rubs, a serious back bar of American whiskey, and '90s-themed cocktails and boilermakers. We'd choose it when you want a loud, unpretentious drink and a feed rather than a polished sit-down dinner.
bestFor: Cheap wings, bourbon and a boozy night out with mates
whatToOrder: The dollar wings are the signature — work through the saucy and dry-rub options (hot sauce, Dr Pepper barbecue, Old Bay, jerk) and the notoriously fierce chilli wings served with a glass of milk. Round it out with a smash-style cheeseburger or the fried-chicken-and-waffle burger, and a boilermaker off the bourbon list. A vegan burger covers plant-based diners.
atmosphere: Loud, grungy dive bar with rock and 2000s pop-punk energy
localTip: Wings are the whole point and priced to match, so come hungry and order more rounds than you think — and if you spot the "idiot"-level chilli wings on the board, that glass of milk alongside them is not a gimmick.
tradeOff: It's a divey drinking bar, not a beachfront view spot or a place for a quiet or family-friendly meal — best later in the day when the volume suits it.

name: Don Pedros Bondi
address: Level 1/80 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A first-floor Mexican and Tex-Mex restaurant and cocktail bar on Campbell Parade with a balcony looking straight out over Bondi Beach.
whyGo: We'd come here for the view as much as the food — the upstairs deck at 80 Campbell Parade puts you above the promenade with the beach laid out in front of you, drink in hand. The kitchen keeps things crowd-pleasing rather than strictly authentic: tacos, quesadillas, nachos and churros built around a serious margarita and cocktail list. It's a fun, social spot that leans into the party-by-the-sea energy of this end of Bondi.
bestFor: Sunset margaritas and share plates with a beach view
whatToOrder: Tacos (the Baja-style fish taco gets the nods), quesadillas and nachos to share, churros to finish — and the margaritas, including a chilli version, are the reason half the room is here.
atmosphere: Colourful, lively and drinks-forward, with an outdoor balcony that fills fast on weekends.
localTip: Book ahead and specifically request a balcony table — the beach-facing outdoor seats go early, and they're the whole point of coming here rather than a street-level cantina.
tradeOff: It's more festive beachfront bar than destination Mexican cooking — some diners find the food fairly standard Tex-Mex and note fillings can arrive on the cool side, so come for the setting and drinks first.

name: Italo House
summary: A lively Italian dining-and-cocktail bar on Hall Street channelling '80s–'90s Italo Disco, where pizza, pasta and DJs run late into the night.
whyGo: We'd come here when we want dinner to turn into a proper night out rather than a quiet meal. The kitchen keeps things unfussy and shareable — pizza bianco and rosso, pasta, seafood and antipasti — while the room leans into an Italo-disco party mood with DJs and cocktails. It's one of the better options in Bondi if you're a group who wants food, drinks and a bit of atmosphere in the one place.
bestFor: Groups and couples wanting Italian food with a party-bar buzz
whatToOrder: Start with arancini or burrata, then split a couple of pizzas (the prawn pizza and a classic rosso) and a pasta like a beef ragu mafalde; the weekend bottomless brunch is the signature booking.
atmosphere: Loud, social and disco-tinged, especially later in the evening
localTip: Tuesday is their "Love Locals" night with 50% off — genuinely the smart time to go if you want the food without the weekend crowds and cost.
tradeOff: The party-vibe volume and DJ nights mean it's not the spot for a quiet, conversation-first dinner.

name: Meidy's Cafe
summary: A warm, family-run daytime cafe on the Bondi Road stretch, pouring organic coffee and serving a healthy breakfast-and-lunch menu with a genuine Central American (Honduran) touch.
whyGo: Owner Meidy grew up around Honduran coffee farms, and that heritage shows in the care taken over the coffee and the from-scratch, wholesome cooking. It's an award-winner too — Best Cafe at the 2023 Australian Small Business Championship — and it reads as the kind of friendly neighbourhood spot locals return to rather than a beachfront tourist churn. We'd choose this when we want a relaxed, unhurried breakfast away from the Campbell Parade crowds.
bestFor: An easygoing local breakfast or brunch off the beach
whatToOrder: Start with the organic coffee, then look to the brunch staples — shakshuka, breakfast bagels and the bacon roll — or lighter options like the matcha coconut chia pudding; save room for a croissant or the pistachio cookies.
atmosphere: Relaxed, friendly, neighbourhood cafe with a family-run feel.
localTip: It's a daytime-only kitchen that winds down mid-afternoon, so treat it as a breakfast or lunch stop rather than a late one — and it's up on Bondi Road, an easy pairing with a walk down to the sand afterwards.
tradeOff: No ocean views or beachfront buzz here — it's a suburban-street cafe several blocks back from the water.

name: Milky Lane Bondi
summary: An unapologetically indulgent burger-and-cocktail bar a block back from the sand on Curlewis Street, trading Bondi's acai-bowl wholesomeness for Wagyu-stacked burgers and over-the-top thickshakes.
whyGo: If you're coming straight off the beach and want something loud, cheesy and thoroughly un-virtuous, this is our pick for a no-fuss group feed. Milky Lane leans hard into the maximalist burger genre — think Wagyu-and-brisket towers, loaded fries and dessert-in-a-glass milkshakes — alongside a proper cocktail list that pushes it past a standard burger joint into after-dark territory. It's a chain rather than a Bondi original, but for what it does it's reliable, central and good fun with a crowd.
bestFor: A hungry, un-fussy group feed or a late burger-and-cocktail session after the beach.
whatToOrder: The stacked signature beef burgers (the Wagyu-brisket-and-bacon showstoppers are the whole point), loaded fries, and one of the theatrical thickshakes or a cocktail if you're settling in.
atmosphere: Loud, neon-lit and unashamedly OTT — closer to a party than a quiet dinner.
localTip: It's on Curlewis Street rather than the beachfront, so there's no ocean view — grab your burger here and, if the weather's good, it's a two-minute walk to eat with your feet in the sand instead. Book ahead on Friday and Saturday nights when it gets busy.
tradeOff: It's a national chain and the maximalist burgers are rich and mid-priced, so don't come expecting a quiet, refined or distinctly local Bondi meal.

name: Neighbourhood Bondi
summary: A tiki-leaning small bar a block back from the sand on Curlewis Street, pairing native-ingredient cocktails with easy bar food like fried chicken, burgers and its signature jaffles.
whyGo: We'd come here when we want a proper small-bar night rather than a big beachfront pub — it leans into a playful tiki-lite theme (pineapple logo, flamboyant staff shirts, carved wooden mugs) without taking itself too seriously. The cocktail list is the real draw: 14 house drinks built on rum, citrus and native ingredients, including riffs like the Ausmopolitan and the Bondi-Tai, backed by house-made syrups and liqueurs. On weekends it opens from morning with a retractable roof over the back courtyard, so it flexes from daytime coffee-and-brunch into a late, DJ-driven cocktail den.
bestFor: A cruisey cocktail session with mates just off the beach
whatToOrder: Start with a native-ingredient house cocktail (the Ausmopolitan or a tiki number like the Bondi-Tai), and from the kitchen the jaffles it's known for, plus fried chicken, burgers or a poke bowl.
atmosphere: Laid-back, lively and a little kitsch — cruisey house music, upcycled-timber fit-out and a DJ booth.
localTip: Aim for the back courtyard on a sunny weekend afternoon — the roof opens up, and it's a mellower daytime scene before the DJ-led evening crowd builds.
tradeOff: It's a block off the beach with no ocean view, and the small-bar footprint gets loud and tight once it fills on weekend nights.

name: North Bondi Sushi
address: Shop 1, 292 Campbell Parade, North Bondi NSW 2026
summary: A long-standing North Bondi sushi specialist at the northern end of Campbell Parade, serving premium made-to-order sashimi, torched aburi nigiri and Japanese seafood bowls.
whyGo: Open since 2010 and recently back after a break, this is a neighbourhood sushi room that leans on produce quality rather than conveyor-belt volume — New Zealand Ora King salmon, Australian king prawns, bluefin tuna and wagyu, all made to order. There's an unusually deep run of gluten-free options and a spread of aburi (torched) nigiri you won't find at the average takeaway counter. We'd choose it for a considered, fish-first sushi dinner a couple of blocks back from the sand.
bestFor: A quality-first sushi dinner near the north end of the beach
whatToOrder: Aburi (torched) nigiri and assorted sashimi at chef's choice, inside-out rolls, and the kaisen or wagyu donburi bowls; udon soups for something warmer.
atmosphere: Low-key neighbourhood sushi spot, unhurried and made to order.
localTip: It's dinner-focused and closed Mondays, with only a short weekend lunch window — check the current hours before a midday visit, and call ahead for pickup if you're planning to eat on the sand.
tradeOff: Prices sit above a casual sushi-train — you're paying for premium fish and made-to-order prep — and midweek it's dinner only.

name: Russkis Deli
summary: A long-running family-run Eastern European deli on Bondi Road stocking imported groceries alongside ready-to-heat dumplings, borsch and Georgian cheese bread.
whyGo: This is a proper old-school provisions deli rather than a sit-down spot, and it's where we'd send anyone chasing Russian, Ukrainian and Georgian flavours you won't find on the beachfront strip. The counter runs from Moscow pelmeni and pierogi to house-made borsch, cabbage rolls and fresh khachapuri, with shelves of Polish sausage, speck, pickles and caviar behind. It has held a loyal local following for decades and still pulls strong reviews for the prepared food and the freshness of the counter.
bestFor: Stocking up on Eastern European groceries and heat-and-eat comfort food
whatToOrder: Heat-and-eat pelmeni and pierogi, fresh khachapuri (Georgian cheese bread), house-made borsch, cabbage rolls and meatballs, plus deli salads, smallgoods and pickles from the counter.
atmosphere: Busy, unpretentious neighbourhood deli counter.
localTip: Go for the ready-made trays of pelmeni or cabbage rolls if you want a genuine Eastern European dinner without cooking from scratch, and check the fresh khachapuri before it sells out. They also deliver across Sydney if you can't get to Bondi Road.
tradeOff: It's a grocer and takeaway counter, not a place to sit down and eat, and a few reviewers flag inconsistency on some packaged items, so check dates on what you pick up.

name: SOY Japanese Restaurant
summary: A warm, family-run Japanese sit-down restaurant just back from the sand on Campbell Parade, with an open kitchen turning out sushi, sashimi and teriyaki.
whyGo: We'd choose SOY when we want proper Japanese near the beach without the polish-and-price of a fine-diner — it's a genuinely local spot where head chef Jiro Numata (previously at Wasabi in Noosa) works an open kitchen you can watch roll, slice and stir-fry. The BYO nights early in the week make it an easy, good-value catch-up, and being a few steps off Campbell Parade it's an obvious pick after a swim when you want to sit down properly rather than grab-and-go.
bestFor: Relaxed post-beach Japanese dinners and BYO group catch-ups
whatToOrder: Mixed sashimi and the teriyaki chicken are the house signatures; otherwise lean into the sushi rolls and whatever's coming off the open kitchen.
atmosphere: Casual, friendly neighbourhood restaurant with a lively open-kitchen counter.
localTip: Come Monday to Wednesday if you want to bring your own wine — BYO is only offered early in the week (and for smaller tables), so it's the smart booking for a value dinner.
tradeOff: Despite the Campbell Parade address it's set back in a building rather than beachfront, so come for the food and the BYO value rather than an ocean view.

name: Cafe Bondi
summary: A bright, all-day Modern Australian cafe at the North Bondi end of Campbell Parade, doing crowd-pleasing brunch and daytime cocktails with an alfresco outlook across to the beach.
whyGo: This is the kind of easy beachside brunch we'd send anyone to when they want reliable eggs, good coffee and a view without a fuss. Run by the Sydney Restaurant Group, it pairs a familiar Modern Australian menu — bennies, smashed avo, bowls, burgers — with a genuinely fun daytime drinks list, so you can slide from a flat white into an Aperol Spritz or Bloody Mary without moving. Post-refurb it added olive trees, a herb garden and kerbside alfresco seating, which makes it a comfortable perch on the quieter North Bondi stretch.
bestFor: Relaxed beachside brunch with a daytime cocktail
whatToOrder: Eggs benedict and smashed avocado are the go-to brunch plates; corn fritters, the acai bowl and French toast round it out, with an oat flat white for coffee and a Bloody Mary or Espresso Martini if you're settling in.
atmosphere: Bright, casual and social, with indoor seats and greenery-framed kerbside tables.
localTip: It doesn't take bookings and runs first-come, first-served, so if you want the alfresco tables with the beach outlook, aim for early morning before the North Bondi brunch crowd fills them; you can also order ahead online to skip the queue for takeaway.
tradeOff: It's a well-executed but fairly conventional Bondi brunch cafe rather than a destination kitchen, and it sits across the road from the sand — you get the views, not a true beachfront table.

name: Hotel Bondi
summary: The landmark 1920s pub sitting directly opposite the sand at the southern end of Campbell Parade, pairing an ocean-view public bar with a Modern Australian kitchen and the more polished Curlewis Bar.
whyGo: This is the big, unmissable heritage corner pub anchoring Bondi's main strip, and we'd choose it when you want a beachfront drink and a feed without a fuss or a booking. The kitchen runs a stone-fire pizza oven alongside seafood and pub classics, so a large mixed group can order across parmy-and-schnitzel territory and lighter oysters-and-ceviche in one sitting. Weekend DJs and Sunday sessions turn it from a daytime lunch spot into a proper late-night venue.
bestFor: Big casual groups wanting beachfront drinks and pub food on the strip
whatToOrder: Wood-fired pizza, the chicken parmy or veal schnitzel for pub-classic comfort, or lean into the raw bar with oysters, prawns and ceviche if you're coming straight off the beach; cocktails at the Curlewis Bar.
atmosphere: Buzzy, high-volume beachside pub; laid-back by day, party-leaning late.
localTip: Skip the ground-floor scrum and head up for the terrace and ocean views, or slip into the Curlewis Bar when you want the cocktails and a slightly calmer room.
tradeOff: It's a high-turnover tourist-strip pub, so food quality can be uneven and it gets loud and crowded on weekends — come for the location and atmosphere rather than a refined meal.

name: Sake Street
summary: A chef-driven Japanese sushi restaurant on Hall Street, a short walk back from Bondi Beach, built around hand-crafted sushi from fresh, daily fish.
whyGo: Sake Street is a small, sushi-forward Japanese room run by chef Yang Yang, who makes his own mayo and soy and hand-forms each piece from salmon, kingfish and tuna. If you want considered, traditional sushi rather than a big beachfront scene, this is the kind of quiet Hall Street spot we'd choose for it. Reservations are by phone, which tells you it leans intimate rather than walk-in-and-wait.
bestFor: A focused sushi dinner away from the beachfront crowds
whatToOrder: Nigiri and sashimi built around the day's catch — salmon, kingfish and tuna — with house-made condiments; the name points you toward pairing with sake.
atmosphere: Small, calm, chef-led sushi room
localTip: Book ahead by phone — it's a compact room and reservations are handled by call only, so don't bank on walking up on a busy Bondi night.
tradeOff: No ocean views or beachfront buzz — it's a back-street sushi room, and the premium, chef-driven approach sits above the casual Bondi average on price.

name: The Kiosk at Promenade Bondi Beach
address: Shop 4, Bondi Pavilion, Queen Elizabeth Drive, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: The walk-up takeaway kiosk at Promenade Bondi Beach, pouring coffee and serving breakfast buns, snacks and fish and chips right on the Pavilion promenade.
whyGo: This is the grab-and-go arm of Promenade, House Made Hospitality's big three-in-one Pavilion venue, so you get the same kitchen's coastal-Australian leaning without a sit-down commitment. We'd choose the Kiosk when you want a proper coffee and a quick bite but would rather keep your feet near the sand than take a table, and its spot on Queen Elizabeth Drive puts the promenade and the beach right in front of you.
bestFor: A quick beachfront coffee or fish and chips without a booking
whatToOrder: Takeaway coffee and cold drinks, a breakfast bun in the morning, and the fish and chips for a midday feed on the sand.
atmosphere: Casual walk-up counter looking straight out over Bondi Beach.
localTip: The Kiosk keeps shorter hours than the main Promenade restaurant and winds down mid-afternoon, so treat it as a breakfast-and-lunch stop rather than a dinner option; if you want a sit-down meal or the Beach Bar, head into the main venue instead.
tradeOff: It's takeaway-only with limited seating and early-closing hours, so it's built for speed, not for lingering.

name: The Stuffed Beaver
summary: A long-running Canadian dive bar on Bondi Road slinging poutine, burgers and Bloody Caesars in a kitschy, Americana-meets-ski-lodge room.
whyGo: This is Bondi's go-to for North American comfort food done with real conviction — it landed on the strip back in 2011 and has kept its cult following for poutine that regulars will tell you is the best in Sydney. We'd choose it when you want something loud, low-key and unpretentious rather than a polished sit-down dinner: rotating craft beers, natural wine and a taxidermy-and-disco-ball fitout that leans fully into the joke. It's a bar first, so come to graze and drink rather than for a hushed meal.
bestFor: Casual drinks and comfort-food grazing with a group
whatToOrder: The classic poutine (fries, gravy and cheese curds) is the signature — the loaded pork versions are the house move; back it with a cheeseburger, hot wings and a Bloody Caesar.
atmosphere: Lively, kitschy dive-bar energy — booths, Canadiana on the walls, a bit of a party after dark.
localTip: It's closed Mondays and doesn't open until the afternoon/evening midweek (weekends from midday), so it's an afternoon-and-after-dark spot rather than a lunch stop — check the current hours before you walk up.
tradeOff: It's rich, indulgent bar food in a deliberately noisy, kitsch-heavy room — not the pick if you want a quiet or health-forward Bondi meal, and vegetarians beyond the mushroom burger and a salad or two will find the menu meat-heavy.

name: Gusto Espresso Bar
summary: A no-frills Hall Street espresso bar and deli-style cafe that's been caffeinating Bondi since the early '90s, built for takeaway coffee and a quick brekkie roll on the walk to the beach.
whyGo: This is one of the original Bondi coffee shops — a genuine neighbourhood institution more than 20 years deep, from an era when decent espresso by the beach was a novelty. We'd choose it over the influencer brunch rooms when you want a strong, reliable coffee and a hot roll without the queue or the theatre. It trades on being a locals' fixture rather than a destination, and that's exactly the point.
bestFor: A quick, reliable coffee-and-roll on the way to the sand
whatToOrder: Espresso-based coffee is the reason to come; pair it with a made-to-order brekkie roll, shakshuka, bircher muesli, an acai bowl, or grab a fresh pie or salad from the deli counter.
atmosphere: Rustic, relaxed, unpretentious — a working local espresso bar with a handful of footpath seats on Hall Street.
localTip: Order your coffee to take away and drink it on the short downhill walk to the promenade — this is a grab-and-go spot at heart, not a lingering brunch destination, and the footpath seating is limited.
tradeOff: Reviews on the food are mixed — some find the plates simple or portions modest — so come for the coffee and quick eats rather than a standout sit-down meal.

name: Parida Bondi
address: Shop G08A, 180-186 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A cosy Campbell Parade all-day restaurant and wine bar doing a cult-followed brunch by day and Mediterranean-leaning share plates by night, a short stroll from the sand.
whyGo: Parida wears two hats well: a people-watching brunch corner overlooking Campbell Parade with a genuine local following, and a relaxed evening wine bar built around tapas-style share plates and an engaged wine list. The kitchen leans on Spanish and Middle Eastern accents (think za'atar-spiced eggs with falafel and tahini alongside the usual Bondi brunch classics), so it feels a notch more characterful than the standard beach cafe. We'd choose it when you want somewhere unfussy that works equally for an early coffee or a lingering evening glass without committing to a big dinner.
bestFor: Casual brunch or a relaxed wine-and-share-plates evening
whatToOrder: By day, the spiced/za'atar egg plates and the Wagyu burger; in the evening, graze across the small plates — halloumi and watermelon, polenta chips, popcorn chicken, sticky pork ribs and arancini — paired with a glass off the wine list.
atmosphere: Cosy, casual and lively, with sought-after outdoor corner seating for watching the Campbell Parade parade.
localTip: The share-plate value peaks after dark from Friday to Sunday, when Parida runs its later wine-bar hours; earlier in the week it trades mainly as a daytime brunch-and-lunch spot, so time your visit to the mode you're after.
tradeOff: It's across the road from the beach rather than beachfront, so you get the buzz of Campbell Parade but no ocean view from the table.

name: Spice Society
summary: A casual, family-run modern Indian restaurant on Bondi Road doing generous North Indian curries, stuffed naans and shareable feasts, with dine-in, BYO and delivery.
whyGo: This is the kind of dependable neighbourhood Indian we'd choose when you want a proper feed rather than a scene — bold North Indian curries, a long naan list and group "feast" deals that make it easy to order for a table. It leans casual and value-driven, with no-corkage BYO and late-ish kitchen hours, so it works equally for a relaxed sit-down or a takeaway carried back up the hill. The mix of dine-in, Uber Eats and DoorDash means it flexes to however you want to eat.
bestFor: A relaxed, good-value Indian feed or takeaway on Bondi Road
whatToOrder: Butter chicken and creamy paneer dishes, the stuffed / cheese naans (the chicken tikka cheese naan is a signature), tandoori kebabs, and one of the shared "Society Feast" set menus if you're a group.
atmosphere: Casual, friendly and unfussy — a local curry house rather than a night out.
localTip: It's BYO with no corkage, so grab a bottle from a nearby Bondi Road bottle shop on the way and you'll keep the bill down.
tradeOff: It's up on Bondi Road rather than by the sand, and reviews note the occasional inconsistency — go for the food and value, not for views or polish.

name: Thainabox
address: Shop 2, 148 Curlewis Street, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A long-running Bondi Beach noodle bar where you build your own Thai-Malaysian-Chinese dish — pick a base, sauce and spice level, choose a protein, and it's wok-cooked to order in minutes.
whyGo: Thainabox has been a Curlewis Street fixture since the late 1990s and it leans hard into its "design your own dish" format — starch (noodles or rice), a sauce from mild to fiery, and a protein, with the kitchen turning it around fast. It's the kind of dependable, customisable, budget-friendly Asian feed that suits a hungry group who can't agree on one thing, or a quick fuel-up when you don't want to think too hard. Alongside the build-your-own there's a familiar spread of pad thai, pad see ew, laksa and Thai curries if you'd rather just order off the menu.
bestFor: Fast, customisable, wallet-friendly Asian food off the beach
whatToOrder: The design-your-own noodle or rice bowl is the signature move; otherwise the pad see ew, pad thai and the Thai curries (green, red, massaman, panang) are the safe casual picks, plus laksa if you want something brothy.
atmosphere: Casual, quick-service noodle-bar — functional rather than a lingering dinner spot.
localTip: If a few of you are ordering, use the build-your-own format to dial the spice individually — it's the whole point of the place and easy to over-order the set menu instead.
tradeOff: It's a block back from the sand with no view or beachfront atmosphere, and the fusion menu is broad rather than a specialist's deep dive — reliable and convenient, not a destination dinner.

name: The Char Rotisserie
summary: A long-running Bondi Road rotisserie shop turning out free-range charcoal chickens and a big daily spread of made-from-scratch salads for takeaway.
whyGo: This is the kind of unfussy neighbourhood workhorse we'd point you to when you want a proper feed without the Campbell Parade prices or the wait for a table. The Char has been roasting free-range birds on Bondi Road since 2012, and the draw is as much the rotating wall of up to 17 house-made salads as the chicken itself, so a single stop can cover a whole family dinner. It has since grown to Bronte and Rose Bay, which tells you the locals keep coming back.
bestFor: An easy takeaway family dinner or self-catered picnic feed
whatToOrder: A whole free-range rotisserie chicken (the Portuguese-style bird cooked flat with peri peri, garlic, Greek or Thai sauce is the signature), paired with a couple of the daily salads and hot chips.
atmosphere: No-frills counter-service takeaway; you order, you go.
localTip: Grab a whole chicken and a few salads to take down to the beach or Bondi Park for an easy sunset picnic rather than eating in — there's no real dining room here.
tradeOff: This is takeaway and catering, not a sit-down restaurant — there's no ocean view or table service, so it's a provisioning stop rather than a night out.

name: The Health Emporium
summary: A long-running organic wholefoods store on Bondi Road with an in-house cafe and juice bar pouring superfood smoothies, cold-pressed juices and hot bone broth.
whyGo: Part grocer, part naturopath, part juice bar, this family-run institution has been Bondi Road's organic anchor since 1996, and the cafe counter is where it earns its cult following. We'd come here for a proper superfood smoothie or a cup of bone broth to sip while you browse the organic produce and bulk-food aisles. It's less a sit-down meal and more a genuinely local ritual — a quick, wholesome refuel rather than a destination brunch.
bestFor: A wholesome smoothie or juice stop while shopping organic
whatToOrder: The locally famous superfood smoothies and fresh cold-pressed juices are the signatures; also worth a look are the hot bone broth, the raw and sugar-free cakes, and Cocowhip, their coconut-based vegan soft serve.
atmosphere: Busy, wholesome grocer-meets-juice-bar; functional rather than loungey.
localTip: Come for the juice bar but leave time to raid the bulk-foods and organic produce sections — it's one of the better-stocked wholefoods shops this side of Bondi, and there are in-store naturopaths if you want practitioner-grade supplements.
tradeOff: This is a grab-and-go counter inside a health-food store, not a cafe for lingering or a full sit-down breakfast.

name: Bondi Beach Public Bar
address: Lot 203, 180 Campbell Parade, Bondi Beach NSW 2026
summary: A big, central Campbell Parade pub-bar opposite Bondi Beach pairing Aussie pub classics with an Italian lean and an affordable seafood-leaning menu, open late seven days.
whyGo: This is the sprawling, 300-odd-seat room right on Campbell Parade, so if you're coming straight off the sand it's one of the easiest places to land a table, a cold beer and something more substantial than fish and chips. The kitchen runs pub staples with an Italian accent alongside sharing plates and a seafood-forward list, and the bar keeps going late, which makes it as workable for a mid-afternoon schooner as a Saturday-night session. We'd choose it more for the location, the crowd and the ocean outlook than for destination dining.
bestFor: Post-beach beers and an easy group feed on Campbell Parade
whatToOrder: Signature double cheeseburger, a pizza or pasta from the Italian-leaning side, and something from the seafood/sharing-plate list; a cocktail or craft beer if you're settling in.
atmosphere: Large, lively, casual one-room bar with a central bar and sport on screens.
localTip: Grab a spot on the Campbell Parade side or upstairs for the beach outlook — the interior floor can feel cavernous once it fills, so the perimeter is where the views are.
tradeOff: It's a high-volume, crowd-pleasing operation rather than a refined kitchen — go for the setting and the buzz, not culinary fireworks.

name: Buckler's North Bondi
summary: A relaxed, community-minded cafe perched above the quiet northern end of Bondi near the RSL, pouring White Horse Coffee and serving all-day brunch away from the Campbell Parade crush.
whyGo: Buckler's sits at the calmer top of the beach, so you get the sea air and an ocean outlook without the queues that clog the main drag. It leans on a genuinely good coffee program (Sutherland Shire roaster White Horse) plus Botanica cold-pressed juices, with a breakfast menu that runs from granola to Spanish eggs with chorizo and a smoked-salmon bagel. We'd choose this for an unhurried morning when you want to linger rather than fight for a table.
bestFor: A laid-back North Bondi brunch away from the crowds
whatToOrder: The Spanish eggs with chorizo, the smoked-salmon bagel, or one of the all-day jaffles, paired with a White Horse coffee or a Botanica cold-pressed juice.
atmosphere: Light, timber-lined and unhurried, with an open kitchen and a coastal feel.
localTip: Come mid-morning on a weekday: this stretch of Ramsgate Avenue near the North Bondi RSL stays calm long after the Campbell Parade cafes have hit peak wait times.
tradeOff: It's a simple neighbourhood cafe rather than a destination diner, and older reviews have flagged slow service when it gets busy.

name: Handmade Noodle & Dumpling Kitchen
summary: A no-frills Campbell Parade noodle-and-dumpling shop where the dough is pulled and the dumplings pleated in an open kitchen, a few steps back from the sand.
whyGo: If you're coming straight off the beach and want something hot, filling and cheap without a queue or a booking, this is the kind of honest, open-kitchen Chinese joint that Campbell Parade needs more of. The draw is watching the noodles hand-pulled and the dumplings made to order, then getting a generous plate for well under what the beachfront cafes charge. It won't win on decor, but the portions are big and the turnaround is quick.
bestFor: A cheap, satisfying post-beach feed of hand-pulled noodles and dumplings
whatToOrder: Our pick here is the steamed or pan-fried dumplings by the dozen, and one of the hand-pulled noodle bowls; the sizzling-style beef and fried rice are the other crowd staples.
atmosphere: Casual, functional and unpretentious, with an open kitchen and quick counter service.
localTip: Grab it as takeaway and walk it across to the promenade or the grass at the north end of the beach — the dining room is plain, but the view a hundred metres away is the whole point of eating in Bondi.
tradeOff: The room is plain and can feel busy at peak times, and while a table facing the right way catches a sliver of beach, this is not a view or a fine-dining destination.

name: Kazzi Beach Greek Bondi
summary: A loud, warm Greek-island taverna a block back from the sand on O'Brien Street, doing flame-grilled octopus, meat platters and Greek sweets from breakfast through dinner, seven days.
whyGo: This is the Bondi outpost of the Kazzi Beach Greek group (after Balmoral and Manly), and it leans hard into island-taverna theatre — white walls, blue accents, bougainvillea and tightly-packed tables that fill fast. We'd choose it when you want a high-energy, shareable Greek feed rather than a quiet dinner, with a menu built around chargrilled octopus, halloumi, saganaki and generous meat platters. It's also unusually flexible for the strip, opening from 7am for breakfast wraps and pastries as well as full lunch and dinner service.
bestFor: Lively group and family dinners just off the beach
whatToOrder: Chargrilled octopus, warm houmous and pitta, halloumi, prawn saganaki, and the meat platter (pork, lamb and chicken) for a group; the wraps are the easy off-the-beach lunch.
atmosphere: Loud, warm and busy — classic taverna energy with closely-spaced tables.
localTip: It packs out and service slows when it does, so book ahead for dinner or come earlier in the day when the same kitchen turns out breakfast wraps and Greek pastries at a far calmer pace.
tradeOff: Prices run higher than the casual vibe suggests (the meat platter is $120 for two), and reviewers have found the desserts a weak point.

name: Medani Bakery
summary: A low-key North Bondi Israeli-Jewish bakery-cafe turning out fresh pita, sambouseks, falafel and shakshuka a few streets back from the sand.
whyGo: If you're after genuine Israeli baking and Middle Eastern breakfast rather than another smashed-avo cafe, this is where we'd point you. It leans mostly vegetarian and the cooking is honest and generous, from bright-green crunchy falafel to a properly rich shakshuka, all at prices that feel from another era for this postcode. It's the kind of quiet neighbourhood spot locals fold into their week, not a destination brunch scene.
bestFor: A relaxed, good-value Israeli breakfast or bakery run away from the beachfront crowds.
whatToOrder: Our pick is the sambouseks (the curried-vegetable one) and the fresh pita, with shakshuka or the roasted eggplant if you're sitting in; the falafel is the other thing worth building a plate around, and the counter pastries and challah-style bakes are the takeaway move.
